title: Inside the failed mission to eliminate FEMA
all_text:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency is no longer in the Trump administration's crosshairs, according to its former leader.
President Trump has made no secret of his disdain for the country's top disaster agency. In the first week of his second term, he attacked FEMA, saying, "I think, frankly, FEMA is not good," arguing that the agency should be eliminated. That rhetoric was echoed by top administration officials, including then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, who controlled the agency's budget.
Other federal agencies have since been stripped down or even eliminated, including the Department of Education, Voice of America and USAID.
But despite his own significant efforts to dismantle FEMA, the man who ran the agency at the time says FEMA isn't going anywhere.
"I think they're probably in a go-along-to-get-along kind of mode," says David Richardson, who led FEMA as acting administrator for much of 2025 and has since left the federal government. "I don't see there being a whole lot of change."
That shift is apparent inside the agency. In recent months, the fear of wholesale agency abolition or mass layoffs has dissipated among FEMA workers, according to multiple current FEMA employees who requested anonymity because they fear retaliation for speaking to a journalist. But the attempts to kill it have compounded some of FEMA's longstanding problems, like understaffing and delays in getting disaster recovery money to survivors.
"Looking back, I think what we saw was an ill-advised attempt to reduce the size of FEMA without fully understanding all the different functions that the agency has," says Andrew Rumbach, who studies disaster policy at the nonprofit Urban Institute.
A recent report from the Government Accountability Office raised concerns about whether the agency is adequately staffed. Parts of the agency that handle disaster recovery are still understaffed and struggling to get long-delayed money to disaster-stricken states, according to the FEMA employees who spoke to NPR.
It's only now that "serious reform efforts" are potentially on the horizon for the agency, Rumbach says, and those efforts no longer include eliminating it.
In response to questions from NPR about whether the agency's goals have changed since the president took office, a FEMA spokesperson wrote in an email, "FEMA remains fully operational and focused on its core mission of helping people before, during, and after disasters. As a matter of policy, we do not comment on accounts in forthcoming books, internal operational deliberations, or personnel matters." The White House declined to comment.
An inside account of the mission to eliminate FEMA
In one of his first interviews since leaving the agency late last year, Richardson sat down with NPR to talk about his time at FEMA and what he saw as his mission while he was there.
Richardson, who served as an artillery officer in the U.S. Marines for more than 20 years, arrived in FEMA's top job "reluctantly" and with no experience with disaster management. "FEMA's not my thing," he says.
Still, he says he was ready to take on the job because he had previously led efforts to cut the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction office within DHS.
"There was resentment towards FEMA. The president's intent was to shut it down or drastically reform it, and my predecessor wasn't moving fast enough in that direction," he says. "I went there for three things: to get FEMA through hurricane season, either shut it down or drastically reduce its size, and get it ready for rebranding."
Richardson says he arrived at FEMA in May 2025 with a plan to cut the number of employees at FEMA headquarters from about 6,000 to no more than 2,000 by November 2025.
"I always think that you can do more with less people, to a degree. At some point it's self-defeating. But it's definitely self-defeating to have too many people," says Richardson. "I'm a small-government person."
Deanne Criswell, who ran FEMA for four years under the Biden administration, says Richardson's description of FEMA as bloated and in need of drastic cuts suggests he does not understand the agency he briefly ran. She agrees that there are personnel changes that could make FEMA more efficient and effective, but "you can't just indiscriminately cut," she says. "It's only going to hurt the person who has the most need after a disaster."
The Trump administration's approach to cutting FEMA's spending and staffing has also struggled in the face of court challenges. An early attempt by the Trump administration to end a major grant program for disaster preparedness failed after a court challenge, and temporary workers who were terminated earlier this year are suing the agency. This summer, FEMA started rehiring many of those who were terminated.
"Dave, things have changed"
Within months of taking over the agency, Richardson realized that, as he puts it, "the focus was quickly shifting."
He says DHS leadership did not approve a plan he shared to downsize FEMA starting at the end of October 2025, one month before the end of the Atlantic hurricane season. Meanwhile, the president appointed a council of emergency experts to make recommendations about how to reform the agency, and Richardson says he started to wonder if the administration's goals had changed.
In July 2025, he says, he got his answer. As he recounts in a new book, Texas Flood: Power, Money, Politics, History, Bureaucracy and Tragedy, a DHS deputy chief of staff told him, "Dave, things have changed," before explaining that the president's council, not Richardson, would decide the future of FEMA.
Indeed, at public meetings of the council that summer, members discussed a variety of recommendations for whether and how to cut FEMA's workforce. At those meetings, emergency managers from powerful states led by Republican governors, including Texas and Florida, discussed the importance of reforming FEMA, but did not publicly advocate for eliminating it.
"I think that's where we started to see the rhetoric start to change about FEMA," says Criswell. "There are so many communities, and many Republican communities, that depend on the aid that you couldn't just get rid of it without having a negative impact."
The politics began to look more complicated, says Richardson. He writes that he supported the work of the council and continued to advocate for major cuts to FEMA, but "over the next few months, each time I received a call from DHS HQ complaining about the size of FEMA, I reminded them I could cut the size of the agency's HQ in half the next day; I only needed the green light."
Richardson says he never got the green light to make major cuts to FEMA staff.
New leadership and new reforms
Richardson resigned from FEMA in late 2025, and Noem was fired in March of this year.
Noem's replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, was previously a senator from Oklahoma and has extensive experience working with FEMA after major disasters in the state, Rumbach points out. Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to lead FEMA. Hamilton had previously served as the agency's acting administrator before Richardson took over, but Richardson felt he "wasn't moving fast enough."
In his introductory email to FEMA staff, obtained by NPR, Hamilton wrote that he looks forward to "strengthening the agency for the future."
Meanwhile, the president's FEMA Review Council submitted its recommendations earlier this year and called for states to take more responsibility for disasters. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Hamilton promised to come up with a plan to implement some of those recommendations. Just this week, the agency announced a pilot program with the state of Indiana aimed at getting disaster relief money to the state more quickly for flood repairs.
Rumbach says that approach is very different from Richardson's. "Those are the kind of improvements I'd hope to see in the coming years," he says. "Compared to some of the more dramatic and draconian cuts that were being recommended."
But many of the most sweeping FEMA reforms, such as making the agency report directly to the president and overhauling the system for getting money to individual disaster survivors, would require the White House and Congress to work together. That doesn't appear to be a priority for the administration today. A bipartisan FEMA reform bill is waiting in committee, and President Trump has rarely spoken about FEMA this summer, even after major disasters, including floods and catastrophic wildfires.

title: Eastbourne roller-skating rink to reopen with free session after flooding
all_text:
My Skate World in Eastbourne is officially reopening on Friday, 4 September 2026, following a two-week closure caused by severe flood damage.
To celebrate its return, the venue is hosting a completely free "welcome back" skating session on Friday from 6:00 pm to 8:30 pm.
Reopening Details & Venue Status
The popular skating rink, located on Maple Road, was forced to shut its doors after suffering a "catastrophic ingress of water" on Thursday, 20 August 2026. The flooding soaked ground-floor carpets, damaged furniture, and impacted the building's electrics. Following extensive sanitisation, drying, and repairs alongside electricians and professional cleaners, the rink is safe to welcome skaters back.
- Regular Sessions: Normal timetables and paid sessions will fully resume on Saturday, 5 September 2026. Tickets can be purchased at the door or via the official My Skate World Website.
- Soft Play Area: The building's soft play section remains temporarily closed as it requires further repair work before it can safely reopen

title: Water rescues and collapsed scaffolding: Storm led to 1,500 calls for service, Toronto Fire says. Live updates here.
all_text:
Crews are continuing to clean up from severe thunderstorms that caused widespread flooding across Toronto on Wednesday.
Thousands of people are still without electricity after destructive winds knocked down trees and power lines.
Several major roadways, including the Don Valley Parkway, have now reopened.
- Your hourly and 7-day forecast on our CP24.com weather hub
- IN PHOTOS: Toronto hit by thunderstorm
- A recap of yesterday’s destructive storm
Follow along for live updates.
Key details
- All lanes of the Don Valley Parkway are now open between Bloor Street and the Gardiner Expressway.
- The TRCA said depending on where you were in Toronto, residents saw between 10 and 112 millimetres of accumulation.
- Toronto Fire responded to nearly 1,500 calls for service
- About 6,000 Toronto Hydro customers remain without power
- The Bayview Extension remains closed between Pottery Road and River Street
Contact insurer ‘as soon as possible’
In the aftermath of the storm, the Insurance Bureau of Canada (IBC) is advising homeowners who sustained damage to their property to contact their insurance provider “as soon as possible” to start a claim.
IBC says that, as soon as it is safe to do so, homeowners should access and document any damage, including taking photos. If possible, assembling proof of purchases and receipts can be useful in processing a claim.
Homeowners are encouraged to keep any damaged items, so long as they don’t’ pose a health hazard, such as wet or mold damaged items. Any discarded items should be recorded and photographed before they are disposed of.
The IBC notes that insurance coverage will differ from homeowner to homeowner. For example, water damage due to sewer backup is only covered if you have purchased specific, optional sewer backup coverage. As well, overland flood damage, which occurs when bodies of waters such as rivers overflow onto dry land, is also optional.
Phil Tsekouras, CTV News Toronto journalist
Precipitation tallies across the GTA
According to the Community Collaborative Rain, Hail and Snow Network (CoCoRaHS), a network of volunteer weather observers that log precipitation in their neighbourhoods, Toronto’s east end saw 54.4 millimetres of rainfall as of Thursday morning.
Etobicoke saw 33.5 millimetres of precipitation by 7 a.m. Thursday. Mississauga logged 62.5 millimetres of rainfall, while Bolton, Ont., saw 92.5 millimetres.
- Alex Arsenych, CTVNewsToronto.ca journalist
Province working with cities on cleanup
Premier Doug Ford said in a social media post on Thursday that the province is working closely with all impacted municipalities in the wake of Wednesday’s storm, while they assess damages and start cleanup.
“We stand ready to help wherever is needed,” Ford wrote.
- Alex Arsenych, CTVNewsToronto.ca journalist
‘Full service today’ on TTC
Due to the massive preparations ahead of Wednesday’s walloping thunderstorm, TTC’s CEO Mandeep Lali said service on Thursday has been largely unaffected. Lali credited all staff across the TTC for their efforts, from dispatchers to streetcar operators to janitorial staff.
“They ensured that the service we delivered, and we delivered well, a very good service, prior to this storm, during this storm and after this storm,” Lali told reporters on Thursday morning. “A testament to that is we have full service today.”
Lali said there were some “pinch points” seen along a few areas of their transit network, pointing to Union and St. Patrick stations. The TTC’s website was also temporarily downed as a result of power outages, though Lali says they were able to issue service alerts expediently.
- Alex Arsenych, CTVNewsToronto.ca journalist
Evergreen Brick Works closed
The historic brick factory located on Bayview Avenue, adjacent to the Don Valley Parkway, announced its closure on Thursday morning online. It says it’s closing as a direct result of the storm and flooding.
“Site access is restricted (no entry from Bayview) while we focus on cleanup and recovery,” Evergreen Brick Works said in a Facebook post.
All events and activities are cancelled for the day, and the Picnic Café is also closed.
It is unclear at this time when it will reopen.
- Alex Arsenych, CTVNewsToronto.ca journalist
Toronto Hydro has restored power to 90 per cent of customers
Dan Smart, of Toronto Hydro, said crews have been able to restore power to about 90 per cent of customers, with roughly 6,000 remaining without power.
“That’s a result of our crews and system operators working 24/7 through the night,” he said at city hall on Thursday morning.
“We’ve made significant progress and public safety remains our top priority.
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
Toronto Fire sees highest number of calls since ice storm
Toronto Fire Chief Jim Jessop said crews responded to nearly 1,500 calls over a 24-hour period, noting that it was the second-highest call volume the service has seen in a single day after the ice storm in 2013.
He said crews, along with police and paramedics, responded to calls ranging from structure fires, high-angle rescues from collapsed scaffolding, elevator entrapments, water rescues, and rescues involving partial building collapses.
“At one point on our app, we had over 400 active 911 calls,” Jessop said.
“The very fact that we have not have any reported major, significant injuries or fatalities shows that the system worked.”
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
Beaches may be impacted this weekend
City Manager Paul Johnson noted that as a result of having to go on bypass for some water treatment and sewage treatment plants, some beaches may be impacted this weekend. He urged people to check the city’s website for updates.
Outdoor pools are “in recovery mode” and some may not open today due to excessive debris.
The CNE is open as usual on Thursday, he added.
It will take the city a few days to get to all of the fallen trees, Johnson said.
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
‘100-year storm’
Johnson called Wednesday’s storm “unique” to Toronto.
“The reality is weather is never the same twice. This was a storm that brought a large amount of rain across the city of Toronto,” he said.
“It is a bit unique in that. I’ve talked to some of our folks, particularly in Toronto Water, and we’ve not seen an event like this that’s brought this amount of water across the city of Toronto. It has been isolated.”
He said the amount of rain that fell, up to 110 millimetres in some areas, qualifies as what they would call a “100-year storm.”
“Wide areas of the city received large amounts of rain,” he added.
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
‘We were prepared’
Speaking to reporters on Thursday morning, Mayor Olivia Chow provided an update on the city’s storm response.
“The moment the storm arrived, our crews were ready to go,” she said, noting that the emergency operations centre was activated earlier in the day.
“They rescued people from flooded roads, secured equipment, and prevented further damage,” she said.
Hydro crews have now restored power to about 90 per cent of customers who experienced outages on Wednesday, Chow added, and TTC operators did their best to move customers safely during “difficult circumstances.”
“The storm has passed and I want to assure the people of people that we were prepared,” she said at city hall.
“We will keep working until every road is clear and every resident has power back.”
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
NB Don Valley Parkway reopens
About an hour after southbound lanes of the DVP reopened, traffic is now moving on the northbound side of the highway between Bloor Street and the Gardiner Expressway.
The eastbound Gardiner Expressway remains closed from York Street to the DVP.
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
TRCA cancels flood warning
A flood warning issued by the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority (TRCA) has been cancelled, but what’s known as a “watershed conditions statement” remains in effect.
The agency said although flooding is not expected in the area today, the amount of rain that fell on Wednesday, between 10 and 112 millimetres depending on where you were in the city, has caused water levels in rivers to rise and flow faster than usual.
“Stay safe around water by avoiding rivers, streams, and nearby trails and by keeping children and pets away from fast moving water and slippery banks,” they said in an update Thursday.
- Phil Tsekouras, CTV News Toronto journalist
Rogers Stadium damaged by storm
Photos from Chopper 24 show dramatic images of Rogers Stadium, which appears to have sustained significant damage during Wednesday’s storm.
No shows are scheduled this week at the stadium, located at Downsview Park, but AC/DC is expected to perform on Sept. 16.
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
Southbound DVP reopens
The southbound lanes of the Don Valley Parkway have reopened but northbound lanes remain closed between Bloor Street and the Gardiner Expressway.
It is unclear when the northbound lanes will reopen.
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
Operations at Pearson airport ‘returning to normal’
Officials at Toronto Pearson International Airport say operations are “returning to normal” following the storm.
“Travellers are encouraged to check their flight status directly with their airline, as some schedules were impacted by yesterday’s storm,” the airport said in a social media post.
Pearson previously said it was deploying undisclosed air traffic management initiatives as the rain started to fall Thursday, which NAV Canada, the nation’s air navigation system, said was causing delays at the airport.
- Phil Tsekouras, CTV News Toronto journalist
City sees more than 1,100 service requests
In an email on Thursday, the City of Toronto said crews continue to clear debris and sediment off of roadways as flood waters begin to recede.
“Closures will remain in place until cleanup operations are complete and the roadways are determined to be safe for reopening,” the email read.
More than 1,100 service requests have been received by the city so far as it continues to assess and respond to hazards across Toronto, “prioritizing safety as well as ensuring key infrastructure such as hydro and roadways continue.”
“Widespread power outages have been reported across the city, impacting several traffic signals. Residents are encouraged to treat these intersections as a four-way stop,” the city noted.
The City’s 10 supervised beaches are expected to reopen at 10 a.m. and outdoor pools may open later than usual today.
Some park washrooms may be closed and drop-in programs at recreation centres may be cancelled today.
All CampTO programs are operating, with activities “adjusted on site where needed.”
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
DVP closed ‘indefinitely’ for cleanup
It is unclear when the Don Valley Parkway will reopen between Bayview/ Bloor and the Gardiner Expressway.
“It is a mess on the Don Valley Parkway,” CP24 Traffic Specialist Meital Sperling said on Thursday morning, adding that officials have said the stretch is closed “indefinitely” until cleanup can be completed.
“Getting downtown this morning is going to be quite the struggle.”
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
Tropical air mass provided ignition for storm
CP24 Meteorologist Bill Coulter said these types of storms are rare in Toronto.
“Toronto tends to not get a lot of these kind of really powerful storms because often the cold front comes in from the west, interacts with the Niagara Escarpment, that kind of flattens out the cloud a little bit,” he said.
“Then as it expands on the eastern side of the escarpment, it dries out a little bit and then it redevelops on the east side of the GTA and eastward.”
He noted that this storm was different as it came from the north.
“This coming down from the north had no interactions so you had these ripples ahead of the cold front that gave wave after wave of ignition to this tropical air mass,” Coulter said.
“And boy did we pay the price yesterday.”
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
Delays on some TTC bus routes
TTC spokesperson Susan Nguyen said it is a busy morning but a “problem-free” commute on the subway, LRT and streetcar routes.
“On the roads, we are dealing with significant delays because of flooding on the roadways there, and this is primarily in the northwest of the city, along Finch, Keele, Sheppard, Wilson, and Dufferin,” she told CP24 on Thursday morning.
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
Storm was ‘one for the history books’
Coulter confirmed that 43.3 millimetres of rain fell at Toronto Pearson International Airport on Wednesday, representing more than half a month’s worth of rain in a matter of hours.
“This is the calm after the storm and it is one for the history books for sure,” Coulter said.
He said certain areas of the city likely got “significantly more” than that amount.
“I wouldn’t be surprised if you hear totals, when they put out the summary, of 100 plus,” Coulter said Thursday.
Toronto will be spared from further thunderstorms on Thursday but humid weather is in the forecast.
The city will see a high of 27 C today, feeling like 34 when factoring in the humidity.
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
Power outages continue
At the peak of the storm, Toronto Hydro said about 65,000 customers were without power in the city. As of about midnight, the utility said service has been restored to about 40,000 customers, leaving about 25,000 still in the dark.
It in unclear how many still remain without electricity this morning.
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com
Commuters should leave ‘plenty of extra time’
In a post on social media, the City of Toronto said several roadways will remain closed this morning “until further notice.”
- Codi Wilson, Web Journalist, CP24.com

title: Two cousins hired a 4WD to find their missing Australian family in Nepal. Then ‘there was no more road’
all_text:
As the hot sun beats down in Kathmandu, Santosh Swaminathan and his cousin Nathan Subramanian take a break from searching for their missing loved ones to stop at a temple and pray.
After they lost contact with Swaminathan’s sister and her husband following the devastating flood last week, they flew from India to Nepal. But as they wait for the army to rebuild roads and bridges into the areas where their loved ones were, they’re getting desperate.
Like other families of missing Australians, they’re now taking matters into their own hands. They’re hiring four-wheel drives and heading into the flood zones to search.
Swaminathan’s sister Chitra Venkatraman, 46, and her husband, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, were among 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash, on a spiritual trip with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour group. In total, more than 5,000 people have been reported missing in Nepal and a further 546 in the Tibet region of China after the flooding, which has killed more than 1,200 people. Thirty-eight Australians remain unaccounted for.
“They are just fun-loving people,” Swaminathan, 42, says of the missing New South Wales couple. “My sister, she is so funny … They are a very loving family. We miss them very badly right now.”
On the weekend, the pair hired a 4WD in the capital, Kathmandu, and headed up the valley. The conditions are dangerous: roads collapse under cars, landslides are common and near-constant rain makes it hard to see. There are long delays, and when parts of the road slide away, travellers jump out of their cars to fill holes back in with rocks. Parts of the valley don’t have power, and there is no clean water or food.
But Subramanian, 45, says they had to try. They managed to get to Trishuli, a town roughly 40km from Kathmandu but still another 20km from where the Australians would have been in Syabru Besi.
“We took a car, food, everything,” Subramanian says. “The conditions are very bad. It’s been really bad – after Trishuli, there was no more road.
“It was a risk, a very high risk. But that is all we can do. As family members, we need to do whatever we can do.”
The day after their attempt, there was a huge mudslide on the road just down from Trishuli, leaving army personnel, aid workers and journalists stranded overnight.
Other families sent another search car up on Wednesday to look for the missing group, which is made up of Canadians, Americans, Singaporeans, British citizens and Australians. They are hoping they can get all the way to the area where the group was staying.
“We are just trying whatever we can,” Swaminathan says.
There’s two pieces of information buoying the families from the group. First, the group was around a 45-minute drive from the area of the border with Tibet which was decimated by the wall of water and rock that ran down the valley. Second, the phones of other members of the group pinged last Wednesday – one as late as 2.30pm, hours after the flood hit.
In Kathmandu, the family have visited the Australian and Indian embassies. They’ve spoken to Nepali politicians. They’ve been handing over any leads to police, and visiting the hospitals as the injured and dead start to arrive from Rasuwa, where the worst of the flooding hit.
Swaminathan is in contact with the couple’s son, Akash Venkatraman, 22, who lives in Sydney with his younger brother. He says they’re being supported by family there.
On Tuesday, the Australian ambassador to Nepal, Simon Ernst, warned families against heading into the flood zone.
“We do understand for those with missing loved ones what an incredibly difficult time this must be,” he said. “Please do be assured we are working around the clock … to locate loved ones.
“And a reminder, please, avoid travel to the impacted area. We remain in the monsoon season; the risk of further flooding is very real and furthermore, access to flood-damaged areas is very difficult, if not impossible.”
A lack of technology available to the Nepali army has hampered the search efforts.
On Thursday, the Australian government announced it was deploying a team of specialist drone operators to contribute to the search efforts. But families are questioning why Nepal didn’t ask for technical help sooner.
Subramanian says he knows the army is doing its best and trusts their capabilities, but acknowledges the technology they have access to is limited.
“Ideally on the first day, they should have actually taken support from other governments,” he says. “Things could have been different.”
In the heat and chaos of Kathmandu, the pair are trying everything they can. Running on anxiety and adrenaline, they are determined to bring their family members home.
“Today we are in a situation where we don’t know what to do tomorrow,” Subramanian says.
“We don’t know what’s next. We are just trying to turn over every stone that we can as civilians. We believe they are still alive, and now we are begging for a miracle.”

title: Bihar rivers swell after Nepal floods, Diara residents flee with cattle, children as water enters homes
all_text:
ANI
03 Sep 2026, 20:00 GMT+10
Patna (Bihar) [India], September 3 (ANI): Water levels in several rivers in Bihar, including the Ganga, Kosi and Gandak, have risen rapidly following flash floods in Nepal, forcing residents of low-lying Diara areas to evacuate their homes and move to safer locations.
Residents of Nakta Diara and other riverine areas said floodwaters have entered their homes, roads have been submerged, and livestock are struggling for food and shelter. They also alleged that relief materials and essential facilities have not reached them.
Affected residents have also alleged that relief camps lack adequate arrangements, with shortages of food, drinking water and fodder for livestock forcing families to make their own arrangements to meet basic needs.
With the flood situation worsening, affected residents have urged the administration to intensify relief and rescue operations and ensure timely supply of food, drinking water, fodder and other essential items for both people and livestock.
A local resident from the affected area said the Ganga water level was continuing to rise and had crossed the danger mark.
'The water level continues to rise. It has crossed the danger mark, and water has inundated everything. Water has also entered our homes. We are crossing over by boats. I appeal to the government to arrange fodder for the animals and food and drinking water for the people as soon as possible,' the resident told ANI.
The resident said families had been forced to leave their homes two to three days ago and alleged that no relief supplies had reached them.
'Nothing has arrived yet. No relief supplies have reached us so far,' he said.
Another resident, Nirala Kumar, said the situation in Nakta Diara was 'very bad' as water had entered houses and people were facing shortages of food and drinking water.
'Water has entered all the houses. There is a severe shortage of food supplies. People have no food to eat or water to drink, and all walking paths and roads are blocked,' Kumar said.
He said more than half the residents had already left their homes and urged the government to arrange food, water and facilities for livestock.
'The government should arrange food and water for us and make arrangements for the cattle. They should set up community kitchens or arrange food relief,' he said.
Kumar said residents face the same hardship every year during the floods and sought relief arrangements for the three months when the area remains affected.
Another resident, Umesh Kumar Yadav, said families were fleeing with their cattle and children as floodwaters entered their homes.
'Yes, that's why we are fleeing with our cattle and our children. We are bringing all our cattle along,' Yadav said.
He alleged that residents of Diara areas were not receiving adequate government support.
'We get nothing. Only the market town people get relief. People from Diara receive nothing,' he alleged.
Yadav said residents were being forced to arrange food and fodder for their livestock with their own money.
'We will feed them with our own money,' he said, adding that the damage across the panchayat was extensive.
Meanwhile, a local shopkeeper at a cremation ground said the rising Ganga water level was making it increasingly difficult to conduct last rites.
'The water level of the Ganga is continuously rising. If it rises by another foot or so, it will reach the road, and cremations will have to be done on the road itself,' shopkeeper Santosh Kumar told ANI.
He urged the administration to take measures to prevent soil erosion and place sandbags along the riverbank.
BJP MLA from Digha, Sanjeev Chaurasia, said the administration was monitoring the situation and taking steps to provide shelter and fodder to affected residents and livestock.
'We are continuously conducting ground inspections along the Ganga and monitoring the water levels. You can see how rapidly the water level of the Ganga has surged. Consequently, a large number of cattle are arriving from the Nakta Diara panchayat area,' Chaurasia said.
He said the Circle Officer had been called and temporary shelters and fodder arrangements were being made.
'Tents and temporary shelters have been erected immediately, and more are being set up. Fodder arrangements for the cattle are also being made here,' the MLA said.
Chaurasia said he had coordinated with the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and would visit Nakta Diara and Bind Toli to assess the situation.
'In coordination with the administration, all necessary flood relief facilities provided by the government will certainly be delivered. There will be no shortage of relief; everyone will receive aid,' he said.
Appealing to residents to remain assured, Chaurasia said the government was taking measures to provide shelter, fodder and food through community kitchens.
'The government is taking swift, proactive measures on all fronts. We are ensuring that no one faces hardships-whether it is arranging fodder for livestock, setting up shelter homes for flood victims, or running community relief kitchens,' he said.
He said Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary had reviewed the situation following the deluge in Nepal and asserted that the state government was prepared to deal with the flood situation.
The situation in Bihar comes amid devastating floods in neighbouring Nepal. According to an official update by Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), the death toll from the flash floods has reached 1,204.
The crisis began after a catastrophic flash flood struck the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26, sending a powerful surge of water, sediment and boulders through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems and causing widespread destruction.
As water levels continue to rise in Bihar, residents of vulnerable riverine areas have sought immediate relief, including food, drinking water, shelter and fodder for livestock. (ANI)

title: Hikers describe intense rain and wind before floodwaters ravage Grand Canyon
all_text:
By SUSAN MONTOYA BRYAN
Like clockwork, clouds build up in the afternoon, the wind starts to swirl and the skies darken. Then the rain comes.
Sometimes it is just a few drops. But on this August afternoon, the monsoon kicked into high gear, setting its sights on a remote section of the Grand Canyon’s North Rim. Down below, dozens of hikers were setting up camp along Bright Angel Creek and admiring the towering walls they eventually would have to traverse on the way back up.
It wasn’t long before muddy water came rushing down the creek. The sound was deafening as it crashed against the rocks, carrying with it tree branches, sediment and other debris.
Violent thunderstorms and subsequent flash flooding are nothing new during the summer months in the southwestern United States. Those in the canyon last Saturday knew the risks, but this storm packed an extra punch, washing out key footbridges and doing more damage to infrastructure than previous decades of turbulent water.
Two people died and at least one is still missing. More than 80 people were airlifted out of the canyon, and the National Park Service is assessing the damage.
Forecasts warned of severe storms and flood risks
A storm of generational proportions — that is how some of the hikers described it in interviews with The Associated Press. Some talked about scrambling to higher ground as the rushing water approached. Others hunkered down under a ledge to avoid falling rocks.
“It was for sure some of the worst acute fast-forming weather I have ever seen in my time, whether it’s in the mountains or marine environments or in the desert Southwest,” said Drew Harrell, an emergency medicine physician with University of New Mexico Hospital who was on a training mission at the time as medical director for Grand Canyon National Park.
Harrell is no stranger to working in austere environments and has hiked rim-to-rim more than a dozen times. He and his team had checked the weather before starting their annual trip. They were more worried about afternoon temperatures stretching into the triple digits rather than rain.
But this storm, Harrell said, seemed to come out of the blue just as his six-member group entered “The Box,” the final 3 miles before Phantom Ranch, an oasis at the bottom of the Grand Canyon.
“It went from relatively clear skies to blowing winds in the time frame of about a minute,” he said, estimating the gusts at 40 mph.
Hikers had little time to act
Within minutes, torrential rains, gusting winds and even hail enveloped hikers along the creek.
“We were concerned that there would be rocks and just flooding coming down from both sides of the canyon on top of us,” said Parth Desai, another physician who was with the group.
As emergency room doctors do, they weighed their options and calculated the risks as conditions changed around them.
“We saw basically the flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” Desai said. “And then we were concerned about a lightning strike.”
They made another run for it, heading down the trail toward Phantom Ranch. They maneuvered around cottonwood trees brought down by the first microburst when they saw more debris rushing toward them. They scrambled through cactus to reach higher ground.
Floodwaters overtake what is usually a shady oasis
Up the creek at the Cottonwood Campground, Mike Sumaruk and his friend were relaxing after a nearly 7-mile hike down into the canyon. The wind started howling, and the rain intensified.
“I jumped into my tent because I thought it was going to blow away and was trying to hold it down,” he said in a phone interview Tuesday.
Then he heard this roar.
“I thought it was like thunder in the distance, but it wasn’t going away. And I said, that’s not thunder, and I unzipped the tent and got out and saw the huge wall of water,” Sumaruk said. “We just left everything.”
The Tulsa, Oklahoma, resident has hiked plenty of mountain peaks over the years, but this was his first time in the Grand Canyon. It was gorgeous, he said, lamenting that he wasn’t able to see more of the natural wonder.
Sumaruk used an emergency phone at an unstaffed ranger station to contact park authorities, telling them he and about a dozen others were stranded. A park ranger traveling on foot eventually reached the group, and they waited until Sunday to be airlifted to the South Rim, where the Red Cross was waiting and counselors were on hand to help.
Harrell shared Sumaruk’s appreciation for the park staff, particularly the rangers down in the canyon. He credited them with moving dozens of people at Phantom Ranch to safer areas before water took out the bridges.
“They mitigated the opportunity for there to have been more serious loss of life or injuries,” Harrell said.
The trail turned into a river
Tom Monroe and two friends set out early Saturday from the North Rim. Knowing it was monsoon season, and after seeing light rain the day before, they tried to keep an eye on the weather — though scant cellphone reception made that difficult.
Monroe said they decided to proceed after one hiker they met told them the forecast looked mild. Another who had just climbed the trail reported the way was clear.
They were aiming for Cottonwood Campground. In the first mile, it started sprinkling.
“Then it started just opening up, holy hell raining on us,” said Monroe, 59, of Flagstaff, Arizona, who runs a business making custom food-storage bags for campers.
The trio kept going, figuring it would let up. The downpour continued, mixed with thunder and lightning. Runoff started funneling down the trail. It looked almost like a river, Monroe said.
One friend took shelter in a small alcove in the canyon wall. Monroe huddled under an overhang that protected him — not just from the water but also from sand, mud and rocks falling with it.
“On either side you could see rocks the size of footballs or beach balls coming down the cliffs from the top,” he said.
The friend who was farther ahead had to scramble up a steep slope, where he grabbed tree roots to keep from getting swept away.
The 20-minute downpour seemed to last forever, Monroe said.
“None of us can really stop thinking about it,” Monroe said in a phone interview Wednesday, safely back home in Flagstaff.
Flooding doesn’t dampen hikers’ outdoor plans
Monroe and his friends already were planning to head outdoors again this weekend, just staying a little closer to home and doing some car camping.
And Sumaruk is thinking about a return trip to the Grand Canyon whenever hikers are allowed again. He will be watching and waiting as the National Park Service begins the arduous process of rebuilding a key water-supply line that was severely damaged, fixing the miles of trail that were washed out and replacing the footbridges.
He said he understands “weather happens” and it will take time for the canyon to recover. Years of research went into his first trip along with months of planning and training, and he is not giving up.
“I’m definitely going to give it another shot,” he said.
Associated Press writers Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, and Jamie Stengle in Dallas, contributed to this report. Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: "I ran for my life": Assamese worker recalls 3 days of uncertainty on mountain after narrow escape from Nepal flood
all_text:
ANI
03 Sep 2026, 20:00 GMT+10
Nalbari (Assam) [India], September 3 (ANI): Assamese worker Pankaj Barman recalled the terrifying moments when a massive surge of floodwater swept through the area of Nepal's Upper Trishuli Hydroelectric Project, forcing him and several other workers to flee to higher ground, where they remained stranded for three days with little more than biscuits and water.
Barman, from Nalbari district, was working inside the powerhouse and tunnel when he heard a deafening sound that initially appeared like a huge explosion.
'I was working at the Upper Trishuli Hydroelectric Project. While working... I had gone on duty, and inside the powerhouse and tunnel, I was carrying out my work. While working, a loud sound came. We wondered what kind of sound it was-it sounded like a massive blast,' Barman told ANI.
He said that after hearing people screaming outside, he came out of the generator area and saw water rapidly flooding the turbine floor.
'As soon as I came outside, a massive surge of water came rushing straight towards me. Mud and water splashed all over my body, and I ran for my life to get outside,' he recalled.
Once outside, Barman witnessed a devastating scene as floodwaters carrying enormous boulders swept through the area.
'Water and heavy boulders were sweeping through with immense force. The floodwaters had risen 50 to 60 feet high. Huge rocks, houses, and vehicles were being washed away. People were crying out, 'Save us! Save us!'' he said.
With the raging waters making any attempt at rescue impossible, Barman and other workers ran towards the hills.
'We realized we couldn't stay there any longer and had to run. We ran uphill until we reached the top of the mountain,' he said.
Around 100-150 workers were present in the area, but the disaster scattered them in different directions. Around 15-20 workers remained together on the mountain, taking shelter near large rocks.
Barman said his colleague Samar stayed with him during the escape.
'Samar was with me; I took him along with me. We fled together. I told him, 'Don't go the other way, stay with me. If anything happens, at least if one of us survives, we can return home and tell our families what happened,'' he said.
The workers remained stranded on the mountain for three days, surviving on biscuits and water. Rescue teams eventually located them and brought them down before transporting them to Kathmandu.
However, Barman said several workers remain missing, including his close friend Arun Mahanta, who had travelled with him for work.
'None of the other missing workers from our staff have been found yet,' he said.
The flood also swept away their belongings and identity documents. Barman said photographs of identification documents stored on his mobile phone proved useful when authorities sought details of the missing workers.
He also credited Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma for coordinating with Nepalese authorities to facilitate their return.
'The Assam Chief Minister had also contacted the authorities in Nepal... The Chief Minister had instructed them to ensure we received proper food and care,' Barman said.
After reaching the Nepal-India border, Assam Police officials received the workers and helped escort them home.
Looking back at the destruction, Barman said the scale of devastation remains difficult to comprehend.
'Near our quarters, there used to be a village-nothing remains of it now; it has been completely wiped out. There is no trace left. Looking at it brought tears to my eyes; the entire village and all our friends were swept away. Seeing that sight was truly heartbreaking,' he said.
Meanwhile, the flash floods in Nepal have caused widespread destruction, with the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) reporting 1,114 bodies recovered and around 3,900 people still out of contact. Authorities said 11,993 people have been rescued as round-the-clock search and rescue operations continue. (ANI)

title: Joanna Lumley says ‘heartbreaking’ Nepal flood could have been predicted
all_text:
Dame Joanna Lumley has said the “heartbreaking” flash flood in Nepal “could have maybe been predicted” as she attended a vigil to remember those affected by the disaster.
The 80-year-old actress, who has visited Nepal on numerous occasions and has strong ties with the Gurkha community, told the Press Association seeing the flood sweep through the northern part of the country last week “broke her heart”.
Dame Joanna joined members of London’s Nepalese community at a candlelit vigil at Panas Gurkha Restaurant in Blackheath, south-east London, on Thursday afternoon.
Around fifty people came together at the restaurant to pray for the communities affected by the catastrophe, observe a minute of silence and light candles.
Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday said 1,252 deaths had been recorded since the flash flood on August 26.
It added around 4,200 people remained missing, including 590 foreign nationals from 34 countries.
On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield told the House of Lords that 36 British people are currently unaccounted for, up from the previous total of 33.
During the vigil, Dame Joanna said: “I think, actually, in this country and around the world our hearts have been absolutely broken by what happened in Nepal.
“The sense that it could have maybe been predicted by all the people who understood that by human activities somehow the world seems to be changing, seems to be getting warmer.
“These catastrophes, the great Himalayan glaciers melting, isn’t something that we haven’t heard of and thought of before.
“When you see the catastrophic outcome, I think we feel completely hopeless every day we look in the papers.”
The United States Geological Survey (USGS) said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border between Nepal and China.
It added that a “glacial collapse and debris flow” caused “subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream”.
Rescue efforts had previously been hampered by fears of more flooding from a lake formed by the glacier collapse which sparked the flooding.
Dame Joanna said having visited and travelled in the country, “it breaks my heart because I know how difficult it is to get around”.
“It seems that we have been warned about this over the years,” she added.
“Now, there are two camps, as we both know: there is the people who believe that climate change is largely affected by mankind and those who just say that it’s completely a natural phenomenon.
“I belong to the first camp, which is that I do believe that what we do here, and the fossil fuels we burn and the plastic waste in the sea and so on, I do believe that is making the world a sicker place and a weaker place.
“And the places which are melting fastest are the high mountains and places, and so the Himalayas are there.”
Dame Joanna is the patron of healthcare charity Doctors for Nepal and vice patron of The Gurkha Welfare Trust, which provides aid to Gurkha veterans who served in the British Army.
Her father served in the 6th Gurkha Rifles, a regiment of the British Indian Army, during the Second World War.
Also present at the vigil on Thursday were Vice Lord-Lieutenant Colonel Jane Davis, former Coronation Street star Sally Lindsay, drummer Steve White and Greenwich mayor David Wardrop.
Panas Gurkha Restaurant, where the vigil took place, has been raising money to help with the rescue efforts in Nepal.
Asked about the importance of the vigil and fundraising, the restaurant’s owner Sujan Katuwal told PA: “It is very, very important.
“At the moment we don’t know how much is damaged.
“It’s a long-term project. Yes, money is there. It might not be enough.
“You know, those farms, those land, all the sand, rocks, and how many years will it take to get rid of those things?”
He added: “I mean we all have seen the pictures, you know, it’s like a movie.
“It did not even have a second for those people, you know, no alarm, nothing.
“And they lost their lives, so many people are missing, so many people have lost their livelihood.”

title: Inside the failed mission to eliminate FEMA
all_text:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency is no longer in the Trump administration's crosshairs, according to its former leader.
President Trump has made no secret of his disdain for the country's top disaster agency. In the first week of his second term, he attacked FEMA, saying, "I think, frankly, FEMA is not good," arguing that the agency should be eliminated. That rhetoric was echoed by top administration officials, including then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, who controlled the agency's budget.
Other federal agencies have since been stripped down or even eliminated, including the Department of Education, Voice of America and USAID.
But despite his own significant efforts to dismantle FEMA, the man who ran the agency at the time says FEMA isn't going anywhere.
"I think they're probably in a go-along-to-get-along kind of mode," says David Richardson, who led FEMA as acting administrator for much of 2025 and has since left the federal government. "I don't see there being a whole lot of change."
That shift is apparent inside the agency. In recent months, the fear of wholesale agency abolition or mass layoffs has dissipated among FEMA workers, according to multiple current FEMA employees who requested anonymity because they fear retaliation for speaking to a journalist. But the attempts to kill it have compounded some of FEMA's longstanding problems, like understaffing and delays in getting disaster recovery money to survivors.
"Looking back, I think what we saw was an ill-advised attempt to reduce the size of FEMA without fully understanding all the different functions that the agency has," says Andrew Rumbach, who studies disaster policy at the nonprofit Urban Institute.
A recent report from the Government Accountability Office raised concerns about whether the agency is adequately staffed. Parts of the agency that handle disaster recovery are still understaffed and struggling to get long-delayed money to disaster-stricken states, according to the FEMA employees who spoke to NPR.
It's only now that "serious reform efforts" are potentially on the horizon for the agency, Rumbach says, and those efforts no longer include eliminating it.
In response to questions from NPR about whether the agency's goals have changed since the president took office, a FEMA spokesperson wrote in an email, "FEMA remains fully operational and focused on its core mission of helping people before, during, and after disasters. As a matter of policy, we do not comment on accounts in forthcoming books, internal operational deliberations, or personnel matters." The White House declined to comment.
An inside account of the mission to eliminate FEMA
In one of his first interviews since leaving the agency late last year, Richardson sat down with NPR to talk about his time at FEMA and what he saw as his mission while he was there.
Richardson, who served as an artillery officer in the U.S. Marines for more than 20 years, arrived in FEMA's top job "reluctantly" and with no experience with disaster management. "FEMA's not my thing," he says.
Still, he says he was ready to take on the job because he had previously led efforts to cut the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction office within DHS.
"There was resentment towards FEMA. The president's intent was to shut it down or drastically reform it, and my predecessor wasn't moving fast enough in that direction," he says. "I went there for three things: to get FEMA through hurricane season, either shut it down or drastically reduce its size, and get it ready for rebranding."
Richardson says he arrived at FEMA in May 2025 with a plan to cut the number of employees at FEMA headquarters from about 6,000 to no more than 2,000 by November 2025.
"I always think that you can do more with less people, to a degree. At some point it's self-defeating. But it's definitely self-defeating to have too many people," says Richardson. "I'm a small-government person."
Deanne Criswell, who ran FEMA for four years under the Biden administration, says Richardson's description of FEMA as bloated and in need of drastic cuts suggests he does not understand the agency he briefly ran. She agrees that there are personnel changes that could make FEMA more efficient and effective, but "you can't just indiscriminately cut," she says. "It's only going to hurt the person who has the most need after a disaster."
The Trump administration's approach to cutting FEMA's spending and staffing has also struggled in the face of court challenges. An early attempt by the Trump administration to end a major grant program for disaster preparedness failed after a court challenge, and temporary workers who were terminated earlier this year are suing the agency. This summer, FEMA started rehiring many of those who were terminated.
"Dave, things have changed"
Within months of taking over the agency, Richardson realized that, as he puts it, "the focus was quickly shifting."
He says DHS leadership did not approve a plan he shared to downsize FEMA starting at the end of October 2025, one month before the end of the Atlantic hurricane season. Meanwhile, the president appointed a council of emergency experts to make recommendations about how to reform the agency, and Richardson says he started to wonder if the administration's goals had changed.
In July 2025, he says, he got his answer. As he recounts in a new book, Texas Flood: Power, Money, Politics, History, Bureaucracy and Tragedy, a DHS deputy chief of staff told him, "Dave, things have changed," before explaining that the president's council, not Richardson, would decide the future of FEMA.
Indeed, at public meetings of the council that summer, members discussed a variety of recommendations for whether and how to cut FEMA's workforce. At those meetings, emergency managers from powerful states led by Republican governors, including Texas and Florida, discussed the importance of reforming FEMA, but did not publicly advocate for eliminating it.
"I think that's where we started to see the rhetoric start to change about FEMA," says Criswell. "There are so many communities, and many Republican communities, that depend on the aid that you couldn't just get rid of it without having a negative impact."
The politics began to look more complicated, says Richardson. He writes that he supported the work of the council and continued to advocate for major cuts to FEMA, but "over the next few months, each time I received a call from DHS HQ complaining about the size of FEMA, I reminded them I could cut the size of the agency's HQ in half the next day; I only needed the green light."
Richardson says he never got the green light to make major cuts to FEMA staff.
New leadership and new reforms
Richardson resigned from FEMA in late 2025, and Noem was fired in March of this year.
Noem's replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, was previously a senator from Oklahoma and has extensive experience working with FEMA after major disasters in the state, Rumbach points out. Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to lead FEMA. Hamilton had previously served as the agency's acting administrator before Richardson took over, but Richardson felt he "wasn't moving fast enough."
In his introductory email to FEMA staff, obtained by NPR, Hamilton wrote that he looks forward to "strengthening the agency for the future."
Meanwhile, the president's FEMA Review Council submitted its recommendations earlier this year and called for states to take more responsibility for disasters. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Hamilton promised to come up with a plan to implement some of those recommendations. Just this week, the agency announced a pilot program with the state of Indiana aimed at getting disaster relief money to the state more quickly for flood repairs.
Rumbach says that approach is very different from Richardson's. "Those are the kind of improvements I'd hope to see in the coming years," he says. "Compared to some of the more dramatic and draconian cuts that were being recommended."
But many of the most sweeping FEMA reforms, such as making the agency report directly to the president and overhauling the system for getting money to individual disaster survivors, would require the White House and Congress to work together. That doesn't appear to be a priority for the administration today. A bipartisan FEMA reform bill is waiting in committee, and President Trump has rarely spoken about FEMA this summer, even after major disasters, including floods and catastrophic wildfires.

title: Widespread power outages remain after damaging storms slam southern Ontario
all_text:
Crews worked to restore power to thousands in Toronto on Thursday after a severe storm battered the city, drenching some neighbourhoods in more than 100 millimetres of rain and knocking down trees as well as utility lines.
Toronto Hydro said it had restored power to about 90 per cent of those who lost it during the storm, with roughly 6,000 still in the dark Thursday morning. Provincial power supplier Hydro One said fewer than 40,000 customers remained offline as of mid-morning.
Localized flooding forced the closure of some major roadways, including parts of Yonge Street and the Don Valley Parkway, at the height of the storm and suspended subway service in some areas during the Wednesday afternoon rush hour.
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow praised public servants and emergency responders who fielded an “overwhelming” number of calls and reassured residents that the city had planned and co-ordinated its response ahead of the storm.
“The storm has passed and I want to assure the people of Toronto that we were prepared. Our teams were co-ordinated and we will keep working until every road is clear and every resident has power back,” she said at a news conference at city hall.
The Don Valley Parkway and the Canadian National Exhibition were open Thursday morning, and transit was running as scheduled, as were city-run summer camps, she said.
Crews will be working hard to ensure parks, outdoor pools and public beaches are safe and ready for the Labour Day long weekend, the mayor said.
“To everyone who sheltered in place, checked in on a neighbour, or stayed off flooded roads last night: thank you,” she said. “That’s what got us through this safely together.”
Toronto officials said they received roughly 1,000 requests for service, while fire officials reported just shy of 1,500 calls over a 24-hour period, which they said was their second-highest call volume in a day, after the 2013 ice storm.
City manager Paul Johnson said the storm was unique in that it dumped large amounts of rain across the city rather than in isolated areas.
“We’ve not seen an event like this that’s brought this amount of water across the city of Toronto,” he said.
“Yes, there was some wide variation, anywhere from about 11 millimetres through to 110 millimetres of rain, but wide areas of the city received large amounts of rain,” along with hail and powerful winds, he said.
“Just to put it into context, that’s what we would declare as a 100-year storm.”
A similar storm hammered the city in 2005, spurring work around flood mitigation and protection, and “those have been working,” he added.
Crews were also out in nearby Vaughan to deal with flooding, water ponding, downed trees and other storm-related issues, the city said in a statement.
“Some roads remain closed, and we ask everyone to continue to use caution and avoid affected areas,” Mayor Steven Del Duca said on social media.
The intense weather brought torrential rain, large hail and the risk of a tornado to wide swaths of southern Ontario as skies darkened over downtown Toronto and hail pummelled neighbourhoods further north.
Video on social media showed large hail falling and downpours flooding vehicles and bus stations, sending people running for cover.
David Sills, director of the Northern Tornadoes Project at Western University, said there was “no credible evidence” at this stage that a tornado occurred as part of Wednesday’s storms, but the organization continues to receive reports and analyze them.
A survey team was heading Thursday for the community of Brodhagen, in the municipality of West Perth, where the worst damage appeared to have occurred, Sills said.
“The team will have a lot of area to cover in the next couple of days,” he said in an email.
The storm also caused flight delays and cancellations at Toronto’s Pearson airport, and left some serious damage to Rogers Stadium, a 50,000-capacity music venue in the city’s north end.
The airport said operations were “returning to normal” Thursday morning but encouraged travellers to check with their airline as some flight schedules were affected by the storm. Pearson received about 40 millimetres of rain during the storm, it said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

title: Nepali survivor recounts 'fight through darkness' to escape flood-hit tunnel
all_text:
Nepali survivor recounts 'fight through darkness' to escape flood-hit tunnel
By Saurabh Sharma and Joseph Campbell
TARKESHWAR, Nepal, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Dhan Bahadur Tamang was at work in a hydropower project near Nepal's border with China when he sensed a sudden air pressure change in the underground tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 1 hydropower project.
Under the industrial floodlights, dust started to rise, the 32-year-old recalled: "Something was coming."
Nobody in the tunnel was prepared for what was about to hit them: a flood wave that had by then already flattened entire settlements upstream on the Trishuli river and was rolling down the valley with immense destructive power that killed more than 1,252 people in Nepal.
Tamang, who had been hired by the project as a support worker, said hundreds may have been on site by the time the disaster struck last week.
"Suddenly, people started running, shouting, and scrambling," Tamang said. "By the time I could have realized anything, I was over a top of a tanker (truck)."
"Once I was up, the vehicle began moving," he said. Water began rushing into his section of the tunnel."I felt again and again that I was going to die."
CLINGING ON TO PIPES
Tamang held on to anything he could grab, climbing on pipes and trying to keep his head above the raging water. He suffered injuries to one of his legs.
"My mind kept going to my family. I thought about home, about my mother and father, about the people I might never see again. I shouted, I cried," he said.
When the velocity of flood water receded, Tamang was still alive. So were others, he noticed with relief.
They tried to make their way back to the entrance of the tunnel, but found the route blocked by debris. The only other option was to head deeper into the tunnel system.
"As we moved, we started seeing bodies," he said. Some people were injured and unable to move.
"There were bodies all around. We were trying to get out and save our lives. Some were crushed so badly that there was no help possible. They were dead bodies," he said.
NOT GOING BACK TO WORK IN TUNNELS
By that point the tunnel was in near-complete darkness, soTamang and the others held hands so as to not lose each other as they picked their way through the debris, guided by a single flashlight.
"It was a long, exhausting fight through darkness, water, wreckage, and bodies," he said.
Then, he recalled, there was a burst of light. "When we finally came out, the outside brightness felt unreal."
The shaking group of survivors was soon surrounded by other people, who supplied dry clothes. But Tamang said rescue operations proceeded only slowly, as fog stalled helicopter operations.
Determined to return to his family, Tamang made his way with the help of villagers but was later transferred to a hotel and then to a hospital for a medical checkup.
"When I finally met my wife, she cried," said Tamang, who has had nightmares since his return, with his mind going back to scenes from the tunnel and memories of dead former colleagues.
"I will not work insidehydropower tunnels again,"he said. "I do not want to test fate."
(Reporting by Saurabh Sharma and Joseph Campbell; Writing by Rick Noack; Editing by Devjyot Ghoshal and Alex Richardson)

title: Nepal Floods: US military aircraft delivers 5,000 specialised disaster victim recovery supplies
all_text:
ANI
03 Sep 2026, 20:31 GMT+10
Kathmandu [Nepal], September 3 (ANI): As disaster relief operations kick into full swing in Nepal following the devastating August 26 Bhote Koshi floods, the United States has sent additional humanitarian and disaster response assistance to the Himalayan nation.
Sharing the details in a post on X, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, who is also the Special Envoy for South and Central Asian Affairs, said that on Thursday, two US military cargo aircraft delivered 5,000 specialised disaster victim recovery supplies, 500 first aid kits, stretchers, and front-end loaders to support Nepal-led search, rescue, and recovery operations.
Gor said that the assistance responds directly to requests from the Government of Nepal and comes in addition to the $3.6 million in U.S. assistance already announced for the flood response.
Countries from across the world have stepped up as rescue and rehabilitation efforts kick in in Nepal.
On Wednesday, the fifth Indian aircraft landed in Nepal in the morning, carrying an 11-member rescue team with specialised equipment and 5.5 tonnes of essential medicines.
Earlier, the Swiss Foreign Ministry said that the country is providing around USD 1 million in total through the UN for humanitarian assistance in Nepal, supporting immediate emergency assistance for affected communities.
Singapore will send humanitarian supplies and deploy a specialist team of police officers to Nepal following deadly flash floods along the Nepal-China border, Singapore's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced on Monday.
The United Arab Emirates, through the UAE Aid Agency, has sent an aircraft carrying urgent relief aid, consisting of 83 tonnes of food supplies and various shelter and humanitarian essentials, to the friendly Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal, WAM reported.
Earlier, the Nepal Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that Kathmandu has begun performing temporary burials for flood victims as search and rescue operations are proceeding around the clock in northern and central parts of the country following the catastrophic Bhote Koshi River flash floods.

title: Hikers describe intense rain and wind before floodwaters ravage Grand Canyon
all_text:
Like clockwork, clouds build up in the afternoon, the wind starts to swirl and the skies darken. Then the rain comes.
Sometimes it is just a few drops. But on this August afternoon, the monsoon kicked into high gear, setting its sights on a remote section of the Grand Canyon's North Rim. Down below, dozens of hikers were setting up camp along Bright Angel Creek and admiring the towering walls they eventually would have to traverse on the way back up.
It wasn't long before muddy water came rushing down the creek. The sound was deafening as it crashed against the rocks, carrying with it tree branches, sediment and other debris.
Violent thunderstorms and subsequent flash flooding are nothing new during the summer months in the southwestern United States. Those in the canyon last Saturday knew the risks, but this storm packed an extra punch, washing out key footbridges and doing more damage to infrastructure than previous decades of turbulent water.
Two people died and at least one is still missing. More than 80 people were airlifted out of the canyon, and the National Park Service is assessing the damage.
Forecasts warned of severe storms and flood risks
A storm of generational proportions — that is how some of the hikers described it in interviews with The Associated Press. Some talked about scrambling to higher ground as the rushing water approached. Others hunkered down under a ledge to avoid falling rocks.
“It was for sure some of the worst acute fast-forming weather I have ever seen in my time, whether it’s in the mountains or marine environments or in the desert Southwest,” said Drew Harrell, an emergency medicine physician with University of New Mexico Hospital who was on a training mission at the time as medical director for Grand Canyon National Park.
Harrell is no stranger to working in austere environments and has hiked rim-to-rim more than a dozen times. He and his team had checked the weather before starting their annual trip. They were more worried about afternoon temperatures stretching into the triple digits rather than rain.
But this storm, Harrell said, seemed to come out of the blue just as his six-member group entered “The Box,” the final 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) before Phantom Ranch, an oasis at the bottom of the Grand Canyon.
“It went from relatively clear skies to blowing winds in the time frame of about a minute,” he said, estimating the gusts at 40 mph (64 kph).
Hikers had little time to act
Within minutes, torrential rains, gusting winds and even hail enveloped hikers along the creek.
“We were concerned that there would be rocks and just flooding coming down from both sides of the canyon on top of us,” said Parth Desai, another physician who was with the group.
As emergency room doctors do, they weighed their options and calculated the risks as conditions changed around them.
“We saw basically the flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” Desai said. “And then we were concerned about a lightning strike.”
They made another run for it, heading down the trail toward Phantom Ranch. They maneuvered around cottonwood trees brought down by the first microburst when they saw more debris rushing toward them. They scrambled through cactus to reach higher ground.
Floodwaters overtake what is usually a shady oasis
Up the creek at the Cottonwood Campground, Mike Sumaruk and his friend were relaxing after a nearly 7-mile (11-kilometer) hike down into the canyon. The wind started howling, and the rain intensified.
“I jumped into my tent because I thought it was going to blow away and was trying to hold it down,” he said in a phone interview Tuesday.
Then he heard this roar.
“I thought it was like thunder in the distance, but it wasn’t going away. And I said, that’s not thunder, and I unzipped the tent and got out and saw the huge wall of water,” Sumaruk said. “We just left everything.”
The Tulsa, Oklahoma, resident has hiked plenty of mountain peaks over the years, but this was his first time in the Grand Canyon. It was gorgeous, he said, lamenting that he wasn't able to see more of the natural wonder.
Sumaruk used an emergency phone at an unstaffed ranger station to contact park authorities, telling them he and about a dozen others were stranded. A park ranger traveling on foot eventually reached the group, and they waited until Sunday to be airlifted to the South Rim, where the Red Cross was waiting and counselors were on hand to help.
Harrell shared Sumaruk's appreciation for the park staff, particularly the rangers down in the canyon. He credited them with moving dozens of people at Phantom Ranch to safer areas before water took out the bridges.
“They mitigated the opportunity for there to have been more serious loss of life or injuries,” Harrell said.
The trail turned into a river
Tom Monroe and two friends set out early Saturday from the North Rim. Knowing it was monsoon season, and after seeing light rain the day before, they tried to keep an eye on the weather — though scant cellphone reception made that difficult.
Monroe said they decided to proceed after one hiker they met told them the forecast looked mild. Another who had just climbed the trail reported the way was clear.
They were aiming for Cottonwood Campground. In the first mile, it started sprinkling.
“Then it started just opening up, holy hell raining on us,” said Monroe, 59, of Flagstaff, Arizona, who runs a business making custom food-storage bags for campers.
The trio kept going, figuring it would let up. The downpour continued, mixed with thunder and lightning. Runoff started funneling down the trail. It looked almost like a river, Monroe said.
One friend took shelter in a small alcove in the canyon wall. Monroe huddled under an overhang that protected him — not just from the water but also from sand, mud and rocks falling with it.
“On either side you could see rocks the size of footballs or beach balls coming down the cliffs from the top,” he said.
The friend who was farther ahead had to scramble up a steep slope, where he grabbed tree roots to keep from getting swept away.
The 20-minute downpour seemed to last forever, Monroe said.
“None of us can really stop thinking about it,” Monroe said in a phone interview Wednesday, safely back home in Flagstaff.
Flooding doesn't dampen hikers' outdoor plans
Monroe and his friends already were planning to head outdoors again this weekend, just staying a little closer to home and doing some car camping.
And Sumaruk is thinking about a return trip to the Grand Canyon whenever hikers are allowed again. He will be watching and waiting as the National Park Service begins the arduous process of rebuilding a key water-supply line that was severely damaged, fixing the miles of trail that were washed out and replacing the footbridges.
He said he understands “weather happens” and it will take time for the canyon to recover. Years of research went into his first trip along with months of planning and training, and he is not giving up.
“I'm definitely going to give it another shot,” he said.
___
Associated Press writers Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, and Jamie Stengle in Dallas, contributed to this report. Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.
