title: Inside the failed mission to eliminate FEMA
all_text:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency is no longer in the Trump administration's crosshairs, according to its former leader.
President Trump has made no secret of his disdain for the country's top disaster agency. In the first week of his second term, he attacked FEMA, saying, "I think, frankly, FEMA is not good," arguing that the agency should be eliminated. That rhetoric was echoed by top administration officials, including then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, who controlled the agency's budget.
Other federal agencies have since been stripped down or even eliminated, including the Department of Education, Voice of America and USAID.
But despite his own significant efforts to dismantle FEMA, the man who ran the agency at the time says FEMA isn't going anywhere.
"I think they're probably in a go-along-to-get-along kind of mode," says David Richardson, who led FEMA as acting administrator for much of 2025 and has since left the federal government. "I don't see there being a whole lot of change."
That shift is apparent inside the agency. In recent months, the fear of wholesale agency abolition or mass layoffs has dissipated among FEMA workers, according to multiple current FEMA employees who requested anonymity because they fear retaliation for speaking to a journalist. But the attempts to kill it have compounded some of FEMA's longstanding problems, like understaffing and delays in getting disaster recovery money to survivors.
"Looking back, I think what we saw was an ill-advised attempt to reduce the size of FEMA without fully understanding all the different functions that the agency has," says Andrew Rumbach, who studies disaster policy at the nonprofit Urban Institute.
A recent report from the Government Accountability Office raised concerns about whether the agency is adequately staffed. Parts of the agency that handle disaster recovery are still understaffed and struggling to get long-delayed money to disaster-stricken states, according to the FEMA employees who spoke to NPR.
It's only now that "serious reform efforts" are potentially on the horizon for the agency, Rumbach says, and those efforts no longer include eliminating it.
In response to questions from NPR about whether the agency's goals have changed since the president took office, a FEMA spokesperson wrote in an email, "FEMA remains fully operational and focused on its core mission of helping people before, during, and after disasters. As a matter of policy, we do not comment on accounts in forthcoming books, internal operational deliberations, or personnel matters." The White House declined to comment.
An inside account of the mission to eliminate FEMA
In one of his first interviews since leaving the agency late last year, Richardson sat down with NPR to talk about his time at FEMA and what he saw as his mission while he was there.
Richardson, who served as an artillery officer in the U.S. Marines for more than 20 years, arrived in FEMA's top job "reluctantly" and with no experience with disaster management. "FEMA's not my thing," he says.
Still, he says he was ready to take on the job because he had previously led efforts to cut the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction office within DHS.
"There was resentment towards FEMA. The president's intent was to shut it down or drastically reform it, and my predecessor wasn't moving fast enough in that direction," he says. "I went there for three things: to get FEMA through hurricane season, either shut it down or drastically reduce its size, and get it ready for rebranding."
Richardson says he arrived at FEMA in May 2025 with a plan to cut the number of employees at FEMA headquarters from about 6,000 to no more than 2,000 by November 2025.
"I always think that you can do more with less people, to a degree. At some point it's self-defeating. But it's definitely self-defeating to have too many people," says Richardson. "I'm a small-government person."
Deanne Criswell, who ran FEMA for four years under the Biden administration, says Richardson's description of FEMA as bloated and in need of drastic cuts suggests he does not understand the agency he briefly ran. She agrees that there are personnel changes that could make FEMA more efficient and effective, but "you can't just indiscriminately cut," she says. "It's only going to hurt the person who has the most need after a disaster."
The Trump administration's approach to cutting FEMA's spending and staffing has also struggled in the face of court challenges. An early attempt by the Trump administration to end a major grant program for disaster preparedness failed after a court challenge, and temporary workers who were terminated earlier this year are suing the agency. This summer, FEMA started rehiring many of those who were terminated.
"Dave, things have changed"
Within months of taking over the agency, Richardson realized that, as he puts it, "the focus was quickly shifting."
He says DHS leadership did not approve a plan he shared to downsize FEMA starting at the end of October 2025, one month before the end of the Atlantic hurricane season. Meanwhile, the president appointed a council of emergency experts to make recommendations about how to reform the agency, and Richardson says he started to wonder if the administration's goals had changed.
In July 2025, he says, he got his answer. As he recounts in a new book, Texas Flood: Power, Money, Politics, History, Bureaucracy and Tragedy, a DHS deputy chief of staff told him, "Dave, things have changed," before explaining that the president's council, not Richardson, would decide the future of FEMA.
Indeed, at public meetings of the council that summer, members discussed a variety of recommendations for whether and how to cut FEMA's workforce. At those meetings, emergency managers from powerful states led by Republican governors, including Texas and Florida, discussed the importance of reforming FEMA, but did not publicly advocate for eliminating it.
"I think that's where we started to see the rhetoric start to change about FEMA," says Criswell. "There are so many communities, and many Republican communities, that depend on the aid that you couldn't just get rid of it without having a negative impact."
The politics began to look more complicated, says Richardson. He writes that he supported the work of the council and continued to advocate for major cuts to FEMA, but "over the next few months, each time I received a call from DHS HQ complaining about the size of FEMA, I reminded them I could cut the size of the agency's HQ in half the next day; I only needed the green light."
Richardson says he never got the green light to make major cuts to FEMA staff.
New leadership and new reforms
Richardson resigned from FEMA in late 2025, and Noem was fired in March of this year.
Noem's replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, was previously a senator from Oklahoma and has extensive experience working with FEMA after major disasters in the state, Rumbach points out. Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to lead FEMA. Hamilton had previously served as the agency's acting administrator before Richardson took over, but Richardson felt he "wasn't moving fast enough."
In his introductory email to FEMA staff, obtained by NPR, Hamilton wrote that he looks forward to "strengthening the agency for the future."
Meanwhile, the president's FEMA Review Council submitted its recommendations earlier this year and called for states to take more responsibility for disasters. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Hamilton promised to come up with a plan to implement some of those recommendations. Just this week, the agency announced a pilot program with the state of Indiana aimed at getting disaster relief money to the state more quickly for flood repairs.
Rumbach says that approach is very different from Richardson's. "Those are the kind of improvements I'd hope to see in the coming years," he says. "Compared to some of the more dramatic and draconian cuts that were being recommended."
But many of the most sweeping FEMA reforms, such as making the agency report directly to the president and overhauling the system for getting money to individual disaster survivors, would require the White House and Congress to work together. That doesn't appear to be a priority for the administration today. A bipartisan FEMA reform bill is waiting in committee, and President Trump has rarely spoken about FEMA this summer, even after major disasters, including floods and catastrophic wildfires.

title: Flash flood warnings issued with multiple rounds of thunderstorms in N.J. forecast today
all_text:
New Jersey residents can expect multiple bouts of thunderstorms Thursday, with heavy downpours the main concern this morning.
Parts of Burlington, Camden, Gloucester and Salem counties are under a flash flood warning through 9:15 a.m. as heavy rain sweeps through the area.
"A couple rounds of storms are moving through early this morning producing mainly a threat of flash flooding," the National Weather Service said early Thursday. "Additional storms are possible late this afternoon and especially this evening."
Some areas have already received up to 1.5 inches of rain with another inch possible during the morning storms. The heavy downpours could affect the morning commute.

In between storms, the sun will come out at times today, with heat and humidity combining to make it feel like between 90 and 100 degrees across the state.
A heat advisory has been issued from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Thursday for Burlington, Camden, Gloucester, Monmouth, Mercer and Ocean counties.
Multiple rounds of thunderstorms are expected across New Jersey this morning and in the afternoon and evening. In between the storms, heat and humidity will make it feel like 90 to 100 degrees.National Weather Service
After a lull in storms late Thursday morning into the afternoon, additional thunderstorms are expected Thursday evening along a cold front moving through the region.
The Storm Prediction Center has placed most of New Jersey in a marginal risk for severe thunderstorms Thursday, meaning isolated severe storms are possible, with damaging winds as the primary threat.
Forecasters noted uncertainty in the timing and extent of Thursday evening's storms. Flash flooding will again be a concern with the evening round of storms.
Any lingering storms should taper off by around midnight.
Multiple rounds of isolated thunderstorms are expected across New Jersey this morning and in the afternoon and evening. In between the storms, there will be some sunshine, with heat and humidity making it feel like 90 to 100 degrees.Storm Prediction Center | NOAA
On Friday, there is a 40% to 70% chance of showers and thunderstorms for central and southern New Jersey, though no severe weather is expected.
High temperatures Friday will reach the 80s, but will feel less humid.
The Labor Day weekend forecast includes plenty of sunshine and comfortable temperatures. Highs on Saturday, Sunday and Monday are expected to reach the upper 70s and low 80s, with lower humidity.

title: Joanna Lumley says ‘heartbreaking’ Nepal flood could have been predicted
all_text:
Dame Joanna Lumley has said the “heartbreaking” flash flood in Nepal “could have maybe been predicted” as she attended a vigil to remember those affected by the disaster.
The 80-year-old actress, who has visited Nepal on numerous occasions and has strong ties with the Gurkha community, told the Press Association seeing the flood sweep through the northern part of the country last week “broke her heart”.
Dame Joanna joined members of London’s Nepalese community at a candlelit vigil at Panas Gurkha Restaurant in Blackheath, south-east London, on Thursday afternoon.
Around fifty people came together at the restaurant to pray for the communities affected by the catastrophe, observe a minute of silence and light candles.
Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday said 1,252 deaths had been recorded since the flash flood on August 26.
It added around 4,200 people remained missing, including 590 foreign nationals from 34 countries.
On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield told the House of Lords that 36 British people are currently unaccounted for, up from the previous total of 33.
During the vigil, Dame Joanna said: “I think, actually, in this country and around the world our hearts have been absolutely broken by what happened in Nepal.
“The sense that it could have maybe been predicted by all the people who understood that by human activities somehow the world seems to be changing, seems to be getting warmer.
“These catastrophes, the great Himalayan glaciers melting, isn’t something that we haven’t heard of and thought of before.
“When you see the catastrophic outcome, I think we feel completely hopeless every day we look in the papers.”
The United States Geological Survey (USGS) said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border between Nepal and China.
It added that a “glacial collapse and debris flow” caused “subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream”.
Rescue efforts had previously been hampered by fears of more flooding from a lake formed by the glacier collapse which sparked the flooding.
Dame Joanna said having visited and travelled in the country, “it breaks my heart because I know how difficult it is to get around”.
“It seems that we have been warned about this over the years,” she added.
“Now, there are two camps, as we both know: there is the people who believe that climate change is largely affected by mankind and those who just say that it’s completely a natural phenomenon.
“I belong to the first camp, which is that I do believe that what we do here, and the fossil fuels we burn and the plastic waste in the sea and so on, I do believe that is making the world a sicker place and a weaker place.
“And the places which are melting fastest are the high mountains and places, and so the Himalayas are there.”
Dame Joanna is the patron of healthcare charity Doctors for Nepal and vice patron of The Gurkha Welfare Trust, which provides aid to Gurkha veterans who served in the British Army.
Her father served in the 6th Gurkha Rifles, a regiment of the British Indian Army, during the Second World War.
Also present at the vigil on Thursday were Vice Lord-Lieutenant Colonel Jane Davis, former Coronation Street star Sally Lindsay, drummer Steve White and Greenwich mayor David Wardrop.
Panas Gurkha Restaurant, where the vigil took place, has been raising money to help with the rescue efforts in Nepal.
Asked about the importance of the vigil and fundraising, the restaurant’s owner Sujan Katuwal told PA: “It is very, very important.
“At the moment we don’t know how much is damaged.
“It’s a long-term project. Yes, money is there. It might not be enough.
“You know, those farms, those land, all the sand, rocks, and how many years will it take to get rid of those things?”
He added: “I mean we all have seen the pictures, you know, it’s like a movie.
“It did not even have a second for those people, you know, no alarm, nothing.
“And they lost their lives, so many people are missing, so many people have lost their livelihood.”

title: The remnants of Edouard provide better rain chances
all_text:
CENTRAL TEXAS — Edouard is no longer a tropical system but the remnants of it are going to give Central Texas and the Brazos Valley better rain chances Thursday and Friday morning.
For Central Texas, Leon and Freestone County remain under a flood watch with rain coming through this morning and this afternoon. The rain will stretch toward the I-35 corridor today but the best opportunity for Rain in Waco, Killeen and Temple will likely come overnight and into Friday morning.
Anywhere from less than an inch to 4 inches could fall, with higher rates possible in isolated areas most to the far east. The Brazos Valley could see up to two inches. Grimes, Madison and Brazos Counties remain under a flood watch.
Temperatures will hit the mid 90s in most areas. Eastern counties will likely be in the 80s thanks to cooler temps courtesy of what was Eduoard.
The majority of the remnants of Edouard will leave Central Texas Friday afternoon. As we move into the weekend, the temperatures will rise from the 90s, and possibly hit the triple digits again as cloud cover moves out and the rain cooled air heats up. It will be a sunnier, hot and humid Labor Day weekend.

all_text:
A Canadian citizen previously reported missing in flash flooding in Nepal has been located and is safe, Global Affairs Canada said in an update Wednesday.
The agency said it is aware of 29 other Canadians and permanent residents in Nepal and Tibet whose whereabouts remain unknown.
“This number may fluctuate as new information becomes available, and as officials are able to establish contact with people in affected areas,” the agency said.
The search for missing individuals is ongoing despite treacherous conditions and damaged infrastructure, it added.
Nepal police are asking families of the missing individuals to share any information about the Canadian, foreign, or local phone numbers of their missing loved ones, as it may help with geolocation.
Get breaking National news
Efforts to collect DNA samples are also underway to assist with identification efforts; those who need to provide samples will be contacted directly by Global Affairs.

Canada is sending more than 18,000 supply kits to Nepal from its emergency stockpiles, including shelters, tools, hygiene products, and solar lights.
It has also provided $5 million in funding to support emergency relief efforts in Nepal.
Nepal’s foreign ministry said Thursday that 324 foreign nationals have been rescued, while another 590 from 39 countries remain missing following the Aug. 26 floods.

title: Joanna Lumley says ‘heartbreaking’ Nepal flood could have been predicted
all_text:
Dame Joanna Lumley has said the “heartbreaking” flash flood in Nepal “could have maybe been predicted” as she attended a vigil to remember those affected by the disaster.
The 80-year-old actress, who has visited Nepal on numerous occasions and has strong ties with the Gurkha community, told the Press Association seeing the flood sweep through the northern part of the country last week “broke her heart”.
Dame Joanna joined members of London’s Nepalese community at a candlelit vigil at Panas Gurkha Restaurant in Blackheath, south-east London, on Thursday afternoon.
Around fifty people came together at the restaurant to pray for the communities affected by the catastrophe, observe a minute of silence and light candles.
Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday said 1,252 deaths had been recorded since the flash flood on August 26.
It added around 4,200 people remained missing, including 590 foreign nationals from 34 countries.
On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield told the House of Lords that 36 British people are currently unaccounted for, up from the previous total of 33.
During the vigil, Dame Joanna said: “I think, actually, in this country and around the world our hearts have been absolutely broken by what happened in Nepal.
“The sense that it could have maybe been predicted by all the people who understood that by human activities somehow the world seems to be changing, seems to be getting warmer.
“These catastrophes, the great Himalayan glaciers melting, isn’t something that we haven’t heard of and thought of before.
“When you see the catastrophic outcome, I think we feel completely hopeless every day we look in the papers.”
The United States Geological Survey (USGS) said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border between Nepal and China.
It added that a “glacial collapse and debris flow” caused “subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream”.
Rescue efforts had previously been hampered by fears of more flooding from a lake formed by the glacier collapse which sparked the flooding.
Dame Joanna said having visited and travelled in the country, “it breaks my heart because I know how difficult it is to get around”.
“It seems that we have been warned about this over the years,” she added.
“Now, there are two camps, as we both know: there is the people who believe that climate change is largely affected by mankind and those who just say that it’s completely a natural phenomenon.
“I belong to the first camp, which is that I do believe that what we do here, and the fossil fuels we burn and the plastic waste in the sea and so on, I do believe that is making the world a sicker place and a weaker place.
“And the places which are melting fastest are the high mountains and places, and so the Himalayas are there.”
Dame Joanna is the patron of healthcare charity Doctors for Nepal and vice patron of The Gurkha Welfare Trust, which provides aid to Gurkha veterans who served in the British Army.
Her father served in the 6th Gurkha Rifles, a regiment of the British Indian Army, during the Second World War.
Also present at the vigil on Thursday were Vice Lord-Lieutenant Colonel Jane Davis, former Coronation Street star Sally Lindsay, drummer Steve White and Greenwich mayor David Wardrop.
Panas Gurkha Restaurant, where the vigil took place, has been raising money to help with the rescue efforts in Nepal.
Asked about the importance of the vigil and fundraising, the restaurant’s owner Sujan Katuwal told PA: “It is very, very important.
“At the moment we don’t know how much is damaged.
“It’s a long-term project. Yes, money is there. It might not be enough.
“You know, those farms, those land, all the sand, rocks, and how many years will it take to get rid of those things?”
He added: “I mean we all have seen the pictures, you know, it’s like a movie.
“It did not even have a second for those people, you know, no alarm, nothing.
“And they lost their lives, so many people are missing, so many people have lost their livelihood.”

title: Inside the failed mission to eliminate FEMA
all_text:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency is no longer in the Trump administration's crosshairs, according to its former leader.
President Trump has made no secret of his disdain for the country's top disaster agency. In the first week of his second term, he attacked FEMA, saying, "I think, frankly, FEMA is not good," arguing that the agency should be eliminated. That rhetoric was echoed by top administration officials, including then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, who controlled the agency's budget.
Other federal agencies have since been stripped down or even eliminated, including the Department of Education, Voice of America and USAID.
But despite his own significant efforts to dismantle FEMA, the man who ran the agency at the time says FEMA isn't going anywhere.
"I think they're probably in a go-along-to-get-along kind of mode," says David Richardson, who led FEMA as acting administrator for much of 2025 and has since left the federal government. "I don't see there being a whole lot of change."
That shift is apparent inside the agency. In recent months, the fear of wholesale agency abolition or mass layoffs has dissipated among FEMA workers, according to multiple current FEMA employees who requested anonymity because they fear retaliation for speaking to a journalist. But the attempts to kill it have compounded some of FEMA's longstanding problems, like understaffing and delays in getting disaster recovery money to survivors.
"Looking back, I think what we saw was an ill-advised attempt to reduce the size of FEMA without fully understanding all the different functions that the agency has," says Andrew Rumbach, who studies disaster policy at the nonprofit Urban Institute.
A recent report from the Government Accountability Office raised concerns about whether the agency is adequately staffed. Parts of the agency that handle disaster recovery are still understaffed and struggling to get long-delayed money to disaster-stricken states, according to the FEMA employees who spoke to NPR.
It's only now that "serious reform efforts" are potentially on the horizon for the agency, Rumbach says, and those efforts no longer include eliminating it.
In response to questions from NPR about whether the agency's goals have changed since the president took office, a FEMA spokesperson wrote in an email, "FEMA remains fully operational and focused on its core mission of helping people before, during, and after disasters. As a matter of policy, we do not comment on accounts in forthcoming books, internal operational deliberations, or personnel matters." The White House declined to comment.
An inside account of the mission to eliminate FEMA
In one of his first interviews since leaving the agency late last year, Richardson sat down with NPR to talk about his time at FEMA and what he saw as his mission while he was there.
Richardson, who served as an artillery officer in the U.S. Marines for more than 20 years, arrived in FEMA's top job "reluctantly" and with no experience with disaster management. "FEMA's not my thing," he says.
Still, he says he was ready to take on the job because he had previously led efforts to cut the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction office within DHS.
"There was resentment towards FEMA. The president's intent was to shut it down or drastically reform it, and my predecessor wasn't moving fast enough in that direction," he says. "I went there for three things: to get FEMA through hurricane season, either shut it down or drastically reduce its size, and get it ready for rebranding."
Richardson says he arrived at FEMA in May 2025 with a plan to cut the number of employees at FEMA headquarters from about 6,000 to no more than 2,000 by November 2025.
"I always think that you can do more with less people, to a degree. At some point it's self-defeating. But it's definitely self-defeating to have too many people," says Richardson. "I'm a small-government person."
Deanne Criswell, who ran FEMA for four years under the Biden administration, says Richardson's description of FEMA as bloated and in need of drastic cuts suggests he does not understand the agency he briefly ran. She agrees that there are personnel changes that could make FEMA more efficient and effective, but "you can't just indiscriminately cut," she says. "It's only going to hurt the person who has the most need after a disaster."
The Trump administration's approach to cutting FEMA's spending and staffing has also struggled in the face of court challenges. An early attempt by the Trump administration to end a major grant program for disaster preparedness failed after a court challenge, and temporary workers who were terminated earlier this year are suing the agency. This summer, FEMA started rehiring many of those who were terminated.
"Dave, things have changed"
Within months of taking over the agency, Richardson realized that, as he puts it, "the focus was quickly shifting."
He says DHS leadership did not approve a plan he shared to downsize FEMA starting at the end of October 2025, one month before the end of the Atlantic hurricane season. Meanwhile, the president appointed a council of emergency experts to make recommendations about how to reform the agency, and Richardson says he started to wonder if the administration's goals had changed.
In July 2025, he says, he got his answer. As he recounts in a new book, Texas Flood: Power, Money, Politics, History, Bureaucracy and Tragedy, a DHS deputy chief of staff told him, "Dave, things have changed," before explaining that the president's council, not Richardson, would decide the future of FEMA.
Indeed, at public meetings of the council that summer, members discussed a variety of recommendations for whether and how to cut FEMA's workforce. At those meetings, emergency managers from powerful states led by Republican governors, including Texas and Florida, discussed the importance of reforming FEMA, but did not publicly advocate for eliminating it.
"I think that's where we started to see the rhetoric start to change about FEMA," says Criswell. "There are so many communities, and many Republican communities, that depend on the aid that you couldn't just get rid of it without having a negative impact."
The politics began to look more complicated, says Richardson. He writes that he supported the work of the council and continued to advocate for major cuts to FEMA, but "over the next few months, each time I received a call from DHS HQ complaining about the size of FEMA, I reminded them I could cut the size of the agency's HQ in half the next day; I only needed the green light."
Richardson says he never got the green light to make major cuts to FEMA staff.
New leadership and new reforms
Richardson resigned from FEMA in late 2025, and Noem was fired in March of this year.
Noem's replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, was previously a senator from Oklahoma and has extensive experience working with FEMA after major disasters in the state, Rumbach points out. Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to lead FEMA. Hamilton had previously served as the agency's acting administrator before Richardson took over, but Richardson felt he "wasn't moving fast enough."
In his introductory email to FEMA staff, obtained by NPR, Hamilton wrote that he looks forward to "strengthening the agency for the future."
Meanwhile, the president's FEMA Review Council submitted its recommendations earlier this year and called for states to take more responsibility for disasters. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Hamilton promised to come up with a plan to implement some of those recommendations. Just this week, the agency announced a pilot program with the state of Indiana aimed at getting disaster relief money to the state more quickly for flood repairs.
Rumbach says that approach is very different from Richardson's. "Those are the kind of improvements I'd hope to see in the coming years," he says. "Compared to some of the more dramatic and draconian cuts that were being recommended."
But many of the most sweeping FEMA reforms, such as making the agency report directly to the president and overhauling the system for getting money to individual disaster survivors, would require the White House and Congress to work together. That doesn't appear to be a priority for the administration today. A bipartisan FEMA reform bill is waiting in committee, and President Trump has rarely spoken about FEMA this summer, even after major disasters, including floods and catastrophic wildfires.

title: Australian drones, telco data sent to help Nepal search
all_text:
Telecommunication data is being provided to Nepali authorities to help narrow down the last known locations of Australians missing after catastrophic floods, as specialised drones from NSW are deployed to the disaster zone.
Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong said concerns deepened every day for the 38 missing Australians, as the death toll surpasses 1200.
Rescue teams from the Nepali army were expected to conduct searches on foot with helicopter and drone support in locations where many Australians were believed to have been staying, Senator Wong said.
The dozens of Australians are among 4200 people missing after a glacier collapse near Nepal's border with China triggered devastating floods across towns and valleys.
"I can indicate that after our inquiries that Nepali authorities have advised us that searches are being conducted in the locations identified by Australia, including (The Kailash Hotel) and the Royal Himalaya Hotel amongst others," Senator Wong told reporters on Thursday.
A team of six drone operators and four incident management specialists from Fire and Rescue NSW will be sent to the Nepal flood zone with personnel from the Queensland Fire Department as part of additional on-the-ground support announced by the government on Thursday.
The 15-person Australian Disaster Assistance Response Team will use advanced drone technology for real-time imagery and geospatial information and mapping of affected regions, where transport routes and critical infrastructure remain severely damaged.
"They will play an important role, flying drones through areas deemed too dangerous for ground teams to search and providing critical information to guide search and rescue operations," Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell said.
The technology has AI capabilities that can help find victims, along with thermal imaging to identify trapped victims through heat sources.
Built-in speakers and spotlights will give emergency crews the opportunity to communicate with potentially trapped victims in the rugged and highly mountainous region.
DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and to contact next of kin where appropriate.
Nepali authorities will also be given telecommunication data to help narrow the last known location of missing Australians.
"We continue to work around the clock to ascertain as much information as we can and provide it to the families of missing Australians," Senator Wong said.
"We all hold on to hope, and we've got to hold on to hope."
There was no change in the number of missing Australians, after five citizens were confirmed safe on Wednesday.
Dedicated case officers are being assigned to next of kin, with disaster victim identification specialists ready to be deployed if needed.
Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.
More than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items.
Australians have donated more than $4 million to the Emergency Action Alliance to support recovery efforts.
The federal government will provide a further $3 million to match public donations, bringing the ongoing humanitarian support package to a total of $11 million.
Grieving community members in Australia continue to cling to hope their loved ones are safe.
"Lots of people are stuck in the tunnels over there as well, and most don't have any contact ... we are still hopeful that maybe we can get good news," Non-Resident Nepali Association Victorian co-ordinator Mahadev Dhanuk told AAP.
"Many are not personally affected, but culturally we feel like one family. That's why everyone is devastated," Mr Dhanuk said.
"All of the community is trying to overcome their own plight and trying to help and think how can we stand with Nepal?"
Australian Associated Press

title: KIRWAN: Back With a Bang
all_text:
So the big S-word is making its unruly rounds again. The big C word – Communism - is now so retro only our president uses it.
But Socialism is back with a bang, though under a new brand, Democratic Socialism! Doesn’t the very sound of it send you scurrying under your bed at the thought of voting in the November midterms?
Having openly fraternized with hundreds of socialists over the years, I can testify that the vast majority are sterling citizens who merely harbor a desire to make rawboned capitalism fairer and more representative.
So, what’s different about these new democratic socialists? Well, for one thing they’re young, and feel they’re getting screwed by the cost of housing, healthcare and college.
They believe that the billionaire class rules the country, and they feel little security in their jobs. From the moment they claw their way to an unpaid internship, they know they’re merely tolerated by the captains of industry and finance who will lay them off at the drop of a hat to keep investors and stock-holders happy.
Many work the same hours as Gilded Age laborers, except that the latter had unions fighting for them; if current tech workers tried to unionize they’d be fired and labeled – you guessed it - democratic socialists.
Meanwhile, the vast majority of S&P companies continue to deliver strong profits, and financial markets are booming – a good thing, if you’ve got a piece of the action.
But recent college grads have no stake yet – except large-size debt that requires annual payments.
Nor, for the most part, do they have anyone near their own age representing them. In the 2024 presidential election, an elderly megalomaniacal Republican was duking it out with an even older, egotistical Democrat, until the latter gentleman fled the field after suffering a senior moment in their first debate.
Dude, can you imagine the rolled eyes in the techie bars of Bushwick, Hyde Park and Silicon Valley?
What do democratic socialists want anyway? Depends on who you’re talking to, but a major ask is a Medicare For All health system.
As anyone lucky enough to be on Medicare will swear, it’s generally a good system, not unlike the Nordic social democratic healthcare model. However, Medicare For All would be hugely expensive and would call for a complete reorganization of taxes, including a hefty surtax on billionaires and large successful companies. Forget about that!
But look at it another way, out of the 38 OECD countries, the U.S. pays at least double per capita every other country for healthcare; yet, we rate almost bottom of the barrel in life expectancy. That’s right – we pay more and live less! Can we afford not to introduce Medicare For All?
Another democratic socialist ask is to root out corruption in government. These young blades do not share our fatigued, and often admiring, tolerance of President Trump’s growth in wealth over the course of his current administration.
Democratic socialists also favor banning corporate and wealthy private donor contributions to political campaigns; OMG, they’d even prefer a return to the post-Watergate campaign reforms. How naive!
What about the occasional DSA candidate who supported “Defund the police” during the social unrest of 2020? Well, anyone who did speak so irrationally back then should do a Mamdani, hastily take back what was said, and like New York's pragmatic democratic socialist mayor, go to a precinct and apologize.
As for “Dissolve the Senate!” As compliant as the Senate is under the primary-threatening control of President Trump, with a gain of four or five Democratic seats, sparks would fly once again in that sleepy abode for aging yes-men.
So, forget about the S-word. The Democratic Party, for all its faults, has traditionally had a healthy left, right and center!
To more serious matters. Over the last ten years of geriatric rule our national debt has doubled to $40 trillion. While profligate spending is merrily bipartisan, the tax cuts and foreign wars of the current regime continue to add to the red-ink flood.
Yet, we must allow our youth to dream; and make no mistake, the November midterms will initiate a battle between young and old, old and new, that will continue through 2028.
Dare I predict? Senator Jon Ossoff will be the next Democratic presidential nominee, a relatively young man far removed from democratic socialism, but one who could inspire all Americans. We’ve had enough kings and geriatrics. America needs a youthful change.

title: Lingering chances of rain in the Central Mountains and unsettled weather for the holiday weekend - Local News 8
all_text:
Chances of precipitation continue into the Central Mountains this Thursday, with mainly dry conditions throughout the rest of Eastern Idaho and Western Wyoming. A flash flood watch warning is in effect for the Wapiti Burn Scar and part of the Central Mountains as isolated thunderstorms continue to pass through from the Northwest Pacific. We will all continue to experience breezy conditions heading into the weekend, making for a nice launch into the summer/fall transition period of early September.

title: Inside the failed mission to eliminate FEMA
all_text:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency is no longer in the Trump administration's crosshairs, according to its former leader.
President Trump has made no secret of his disdain for the country's top disaster agency. In the first week of his second term, he attacked FEMA, saying, "I think, frankly, FEMA is not good," arguing that the agency should be eliminated. That rhetoric was echoed by top administration officials, including then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, who controlled the agency's budget.
Other federal agencies have since been stripped down or even eliminated, including the Department of Education, Voice of America and USAID.
But despite his own significant efforts to dismantle FEMA, the man who ran the agency at the time says FEMA isn't going anywhere.
"I think they're probably in a go-along-to-get-along kind of mode," says David Richardson, who led FEMA as acting administrator for much of 2025 and has since left the federal government. "I don't see there being a whole lot of change."
That shift is apparent inside the agency. In recent months, the fear of wholesale agency abolition or mass layoffs has dissipated among FEMA workers, according to multiple current FEMA employees who requested anonymity because they fear retaliation for speaking to a journalist. But the attempts to kill it have compounded some of FEMA's longstanding problems, like understaffing and delays in getting disaster recovery money to survivors.
"Looking back, I think what we saw was an ill-advised attempt to reduce the size of FEMA without fully understanding all the different functions that the agency has," says Andrew Rumbach, who studies disaster policy at the nonprofit Urban Institute.
A recent report from the Government Accountability Office raised concerns about whether the agency is adequately staffed. Parts of the agency that handle disaster recovery are still understaffed and struggling to get long-delayed money to disaster-stricken states, according to the FEMA employees who spoke to NPR.
It's only now that "serious reform efforts" are potentially on the horizon for the agency, Rumbach says, and those efforts no longer include eliminating it.
In response to questions from NPR about whether the agency's goals have changed since the president took office, a FEMA spokesperson wrote in an email, "FEMA remains fully operational and focused on its core mission of helping people before, during, and after disasters. As a matter of policy, we do not comment on accounts in forthcoming books, internal operational deliberations, or personnel matters." The White House declined to comment.
An inside account of the mission to eliminate FEMA
In one of his first interviews since leaving the agency late last year, Richardson sat down with NPR to talk about his time at FEMA and what he saw as his mission while he was there.
Richardson, who served as an artillery officer in the U.S. Marines for more than 20 years, arrived in FEMA's top job "reluctantly" and with no experience with disaster management. "FEMA's not my thing," he says.
Still, he says he was ready to take on the job because he had previously led efforts to cut the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction office within DHS.
"There was resentment towards FEMA. The president's intent was to shut it down or drastically reform it, and my predecessor wasn't moving fast enough in that direction," he says. "I went there for three things: to get FEMA through hurricane season, either shut it down or drastically reduce its size, and get it ready for rebranding."
Richardson says he arrived at FEMA in May 2025 with a plan to cut the number of employees at FEMA headquarters from about 6,000 to no more than 2,000 by November 2025.
"I always think that you can do more with less people, to a degree. At some point it's self-defeating. But it's definitely self-defeating to have too many people," says Richardson. "I'm a small-government person."
Deanne Criswell, who ran FEMA for four years under the Biden administration, says Richardson's description of FEMA as bloated and in need of drastic cuts suggests he does not understand the agency he briefly ran. She agrees that there are personnel changes that could make FEMA more efficient and effective, but "you can't just indiscriminately cut," she says. "It's only going to hurt the person who has the most need after a disaster."
The Trump administration's approach to cutting FEMA's spending and staffing has also struggled in the face of court challenges. An early attempt by the Trump administration to end a major grant program for disaster preparedness failed after a court challenge, and temporary workers who were terminated earlier this year are suing the agency. This summer, FEMA started rehiring many of those who were terminated.
"Dave, things have changed"
Within months of taking over the agency, Richardson realized that, as he puts it, "the focus was quickly shifting."
He says DHS leadership did not approve a plan he shared to downsize FEMA starting at the end of October 2025, one month before the end of the Atlantic hurricane season. Meanwhile, the president appointed a council of emergency experts to make recommendations about how to reform the agency, and Richardson says he started to wonder if the administration's goals had changed.
In July 2025, he says, he got his answer. As he recounts in a new book, Texas Flood: Power, Money, Politics, History, Bureaucracy and Tragedy, a DHS deputy chief of staff told him, "Dave, things have changed," before explaining that the president's council, not Richardson, would decide the future of FEMA.
Indeed, at public meetings of the council that summer, members discussed a variety of recommendations for whether and how to cut FEMA's workforce. At those meetings, emergency managers from powerful states led by Republican governors, including Texas and Florida, discussed the importance of reforming FEMA, but did not publicly advocate for eliminating it.
"I think that's where we started to see the rhetoric start to change about FEMA," says Criswell. "There are so many communities, and many Republican communities, that depend on the aid that you couldn't just get rid of it without having a negative impact."
The politics began to look more complicated, says Richardson. He writes that he supported the work of the council and continued to advocate for major cuts to FEMA, but "over the next few months, each time I received a call from DHS HQ complaining about the size of FEMA, I reminded them I could cut the size of the agency's HQ in half the next day; I only needed the green light."
Richardson says he never got the green light to make major cuts to FEMA staff.
New leadership and new reforms
Richardson resigned from FEMA in late 2025, and Noem was fired in March of this year.
Noem's replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, was previously a senator from Oklahoma and has extensive experience working with FEMA after major disasters in the state, Rumbach points out. Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to lead FEMA. Hamilton had previously served as the agency's acting administrator before Richardson took over, but Richardson felt he "wasn't moving fast enough."
In his introductory email to FEMA staff, obtained by NPR, Hamilton wrote that he looks forward to "strengthening the agency for the future."
Meanwhile, the president's FEMA Review Council submitted its recommendations earlier this year and called for states to take more responsibility for disasters. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Hamilton promised to come up with a plan to implement some of those recommendations. Just this week, the agency announced a pilot program with the state of Indiana aimed at getting disaster relief money to the state more quickly for flood repairs.
Rumbach says that approach is very different from Richardson's. "Those are the kind of improvements I'd hope to see in the coming years," he says. "Compared to some of the more dramatic and draconian cuts that were being recommended."
But many of the most sweeping FEMA reforms, such as making the agency report directly to the president and overhauling the system for getting money to individual disaster survivors, would require the White House and Congress to work together. That doesn't appear to be a priority for the administration today. A bipartisan FEMA reform bill is waiting in committee, and President Trump has rarely spoken about FEMA this summer, even after major disasters, including floods and catastrophic wildfires.

title: Confused by rain forecasts? Here's how to make sense of them
all_text:
Nairobi residents shield themselves from the rain in the city centre on February 22, 2026.
More than 400mm of rain. Above-average rainfall. Heavy rains or normal rainfall. By now, these are familiar words. They appear in weather forecasts, climate outlooks and advisories.
As the country prepares for the October-November-December rainfall season, which meteorologists say is already being influenced by “Very strong” El Niño conditions, many people are keeping tabs on the daily advisories.
A weather update that was recently sent by the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA).
You might read them and think, well, it is going to rain a lot. You might even start to make plans around the forecast because you read some 400 mm somewhere, and that must mean a lot of rain.
Or does it?
But have you ever wondered what some of these terms mean? When a forecast says an area could receive more than 400mm of rain, what does the “mm” actually mean? How much rain is that? And when meteorologists say rainfall will be “above average”, what are they comparing it with?
Hannah Kimani, assistant director, Public Weather Services at the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority, breaks down some of the terms we hear in weather forecasts.
What does mm in rainfall mean?
One millimetre of rainfall is equivalent to one litre of water falling over an area of one square metre, a space measuring one metre by one metre.
When weather forecasters say 20 or 50 millimetres, for example, you are basically taking one litre of water and pouring it in that one square metre space.
But, here’s the thing: the impact of rainfall is guided by what the 50 litres of water will do to that small space that is just one square metre.
With that, you can begin to understand what meteorological services mean when they give us a certain amount of rainfall, and what impact that amount of rain could have across different sectors.
Notably, it’s important to understand the climatology of an area because the impact is pegged on that. For instance, 20mm of rainfall in Nairobi will not have the same impact as 20mm in an area like Kakamega.
The reason is that Nairobi is highly populated and largely urban, with extensive areas covered in concrete and other impermeable surfaces. There are also drainage challenges. So when it rains, the water has nowhere to percolate into the ground and can quickly flood the streets.
Compare that with somewhere else with more vegetation and open ground. The same amount of rainfall may be absorbed into the soil rather than becoming stagnant water or running off into streets.
So, one needs to understand not just an area's climatology, but also its exposure and vulnerability.
What is normal rainfall?
When meteorologists talk about “normal” rainfall, they are comparing the expected amount of rain with what an area has historically received.
They use what is called the Long-Term Mean (LTM), which is the average rainfall recorded over a 30-year period. The LTM can be calculated for different periods, including daily, weekly, monthly or seasonal rainfall.
Rainfall is considered normal when it falls between 75 and 125 per cent of the LTM. Anything below 75 per cent is classified as below-normal rainfall, while anything above 125 per cent is considered above-normal rainfall.
For example, if a station normally receives an average of 600mm of rain during the October-November-December season, rainfall between 450mm and 750mm would be considered normal. Less than 450mm would be below normal, while more than 750mm would be above normal.
So when a forecast says an area is likely to receive “above-normal rainfall”, it doesn't simply mean a lot of rain will fall. It means the expected rainfall is more than 125 per cent of what that area has historically received during that particular period.
Does below-normal rainfall mean there will be no rain?
Not at all. This simply means an area is expected to receive less rain than it normally does during a particular period, such as a month or a season.
That does not mean the skies will remain dry. It could still rain, but the total amount may be lower than usual for that time of year. In some cases, an area may experience occasional rainfall but receive very little overall. In others, heavy storms may occur over a short period, followed by prolonged dry spells.
Does above-normal rainfall mean it will rain all the time?
No. If an area receives 250 mm of rainfall, receiving 700 mm means it received more rain than it normally does during a particular period, such as a month or a season.
It does not necessarily mean it will rain every day. An area could have prolonged wet spells with only a few dry days in between. It could also experience intense storms over a short period, followed by several dry days.
What matters is the total amount of rainfall received over the period. Even with dry spells in between, rainfall can still be classified as above normal if the cumulative amount is higher than usual.

Noem's replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, was previously a senator from Oklahoma and has extensive experience working with FEMA after major disasters in the state, Rumbach points out. Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to lead FEMA. Hamilton had previously served as the agency's acting administrator before Richardson took over, but Richardson felt he "wasn't moving fast enough."
In his introductory email to FEMA staff, obtained by NPR, Hamilton wrote that he looks forward to "strengthening the agency for the future."
Meanwhile, the president's FEMA Review Council submitted its recommendations earlier this year and called for states to take more responsibility for disasters. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Hamilton promised to come up with a plan to implement some of those recommendations. Just this week, the agency announced a pilot program with the state of Indiana aimed at getting disaster relief money to the state more quickly for flood repairs.
Rumbach says that approach is very different from Richardson's. "Those are the kind of improvements I'd hope to see in the coming years," he says. "Compared to some of the more dramatic and draconian cuts that were being recommended."
But many of the most sweeping FEMA reforms, such as making the agency report directly to the president and overhauling the system for getting money to individual disaster survivors, would require the White House and Congress to work together. That doesn't appear to be a priority for the administration today. A bipartisan FEMA reform bill is waiting in committee, and President Trump has rarely spoken about FEMA this summer, even after major disasters, including floods and catastrophic wildfires.
