title: Delta Caucus secures $158.2 million for Delta levees
all_text:
SACRAMENTO — The California Legislature Wednesday approved $90.2 million to protect the Delta and fortify its aging levees, along with up to $68 million to safeguard the State Water Project’s California Aqueduct and canals.
The funding for the levees — which are being undermined by the over-drafting of groundwater — was secured by the California Legislative Delta Caucus.
“Today’s vote was truly historic. California’s water wars may finally be over,” said State Sen. Jerry McNerney, who serves as co-chair of the caucus.
“Today we joined together, North and South, environmental groups and State Water Contractors, to support vital projects that will protect California’s water and the Delta, while also benefitting the entire state.”
“But we’re not done. This historic investment is just a downpayment. In the years to come, we need to continue to protect California’s primary supply of freshwater.”
The budget funding allocation was supported by the environmental group Restore the Delta and State Water Contractors, which receive water from the State Water Project (SWP).
Together, the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta and the SWP make up California’s primary water system, providing freshwater supplies to 27 million people, businesses, and farms in the Central Valley, the Bay Area, and Southern California. The Delta also supports a vibrantly diverse ecosystem of plants and animals.
The funding will come from Proposition 4, the $10 billion bond measure approved by California voters in 2024. Gov. Gavin Newsom is expected to sign the budget bill in the days ahead.
Of the $90.2 million for the Delta, $75 million will be for projects that repair levees and improve flood protection and climate resiliency.
In addition, the budget allocates $15.2 million to the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta Conservancy to reduce the risks of climate change impacts on communities, fish and wildlife, and natural resources.
Many of the Delta’s critical levees date to the 1800s and are at risk of breaching because they no longer meet the US Army Corp of Engineers safety standards. Making the necessary levee improvements will cost, in total, about $3.24 billion.
The vote also included up to $68 million to repair SWP’s California Aqueduct and canals, which are being impacted by sinking land. Over-pumping of groundwater has led to significant land subsidence along the California Aqueduct, which delivers water from the Delta to much of the state.
If not repaired, subsidence threatens to reduce the water carrying capacity of the SWP by 87% by 2040. Subsidence repairs to the SWP are estimated to cost about $3 billion over 20 years.
The legislature also approval was $5 million to acquire Jersey Island in the Delta and repair its levees.
The island sits in a particularly important spot in the western Delta, where a levee failure could threaten the water quality and water access that millions of Californians depend on.
By acquiring this island, the state can ease the pressure on its levees, guard against saltwater rushing in, and open the door to restoring critical wetlands.
In addition, earlier this year, the budget included $6 million to address the invasive golden mussel infestation in the Delta. The request was also a Delta Caucus priority, championed by Assemblymember Rhodesia Ransom, D-Stockton.

title: Australian drones, telco data sent to help Nepal search
all_text:
Telecommunication data is being provided to Nepali authorities to help narrow down the last known locations of Australians missing after catastrophic floods, as specialised drones from NSW are deployed to the disaster zone.
Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong said concerns deepened every day for the 38 missing Australians, as the death toll surpasses 1200.
Rescue teams from the Nepali army were expected to conduct searches on foot with helicopter and drone support in locations where many Australians were believed to have been staying, Senator Wong said.
The dozens of Australians are among 4200 people missing after a glacier collapse near Nepal's border with China triggered devastating floods across towns and valleys.
"I can indicate that after our inquiries that Nepali authorities have advised us that searches are being conducted in the locations identified by Australia, including (The Kailash Hotel) and the Royal Himalaya Hotel amongst others," Senator Wong told reporters on Thursday.
A team of six drone operators and four incident management specialists from Fire and Rescue NSW will be sent to the Nepal flood zone with personnel from the Queensland Fire Department as part of additional on-the-ground support announced by the government on Thursday.
The 15-person Australian Disaster Assistance Response Team will use advanced drone technology for real-time imagery and geospatial information and mapping of affected regions, where transport routes and critical infrastructure remain severely damaged.
"They will play an important role, flying drones through areas deemed too dangerous for ground teams to search and providing critical information to guide search and rescue operations," Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell said.
The technology has AI capabilities that can help find victims, along with thermal imaging to identify trapped victims through heat sources.
Built-in speakers and spotlights will give emergency crews the opportunity to communicate with potentially trapped victims in the rugged and highly mountainous region.
DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and to contact next of kin where appropriate.
Nepali authorities will also be given telecommunication data to help narrow the last known location of missing Australians.
"We continue to work around the clock to ascertain as much information as we can and provide it to the families of missing Australians," Senator Wong said.
"We all hold on to hope, and we've got to hold on to hope."
There was no change in the number of missing Australians, after five citizens were confirmed safe on Wednesday.
Dedicated case officers are being assigned to next of kin, with disaster victim identification specialists ready to be deployed if needed.
Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.
More than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items.
Australians have donated more than $4 million to the Emergency Action Alliance to support recovery efforts.
The federal government will provide a further $3 million to match public donations, bringing the ongoing humanitarian support package to a total of $11 million.
Grieving community members in Australia continue to cling to hope their loved ones are safe.
"Lots of people are stuck in the tunnels over there as well, and most don't have any contact ... we are still hopeful that maybe we can get good news," Non-Resident Nepali Association Victorian co-ordinator Mahadev Dhanuk told AAP.
"Many are not personally affected, but culturally we feel like one family. That's why everyone is devastated," Mr Dhanuk said.
"All of the community is trying to overcome their own plight and trying to help and think how can we stand with Nepal?"
Australian Associated Press

title: Flood situation in Odisha shows gradual improvement as river levels fall across the State
all_text:
The flood situation in Odisha continues to show gradual improvement, with river levels across major rivers indicating a falling trend and rainfall activity reducing significantly.
Relief, response, and restoration measures remain in force as the State Government coordinates closely with district administrations.
According to the latest reports, Jajpur, Mayurbhanj, and Baleshwar remain affected:
- Jajpur: Dasarathpur block affected; 19 GPs and 62 villages impacted. 22 relief camps operational, covering 7,745 beneficiaries.
- Mayurbhanj: 21 blocks, 53 GPs, 97 villages, and two Baripada Municipality wards affected. 29 relief camps operational, covering 10,501 beneficiaries. 104 houses damaged; 9 polythene rolls distributed.
- Baleshwar: Five blocks affected—Bhogarai, Baliapala, Basta, Remuna, and Jaleshwar—covering 41 GPs and 214 villages. 72 relief camps are operational, covering 35,740 beneficiaries.
A total of 47 response teams are deployed today, including 21 ODRAF, 4 NDRF, and 22 Fire & Emergency Services teams.
At present, the Subarnarekha River at Rajghat is the only river flowing above danger level at 10.84 m, though it is showing a falling trend. Other rivers including the Mahanadi, IB, Brahmani, Baitarani, Burhabalanga, Vansadhara, and Jalaka are also receding.
The Hirakud reservoir stood at 627.29 ft with inflow of 1,41,962 cusecs and outflow of 78,429 cusecs through four open gates.
The IMD has forecast thunderstorms with lightning and gusty winds (30–40 kmph) in districts under Yellow Warning, including Baleshwar, Bhadrak, Jajpur, Kendrapada, Jagatsinghapur, Cuttack, Kendujhar, and Mayurbhanj.
Authorities have urged people to remain cautious against localised flooding, waterlogging, and possible damage to roads, crops, and vulnerable structures. Relief camps, cattle feed supply, and restoration measures continue until normalcy returns.
The State Emergency Operation Centre maintains round-the-clock monitoring in coordination with all DEOCs, ensuring preparedness and timely support to affected communities.

title: Julie Cole Finds 36.5% Higher El Niño Variability in Galápagos Corals — Exceptional El Niño Weather Pattern - El-Balad.com
all_text:
Julie Cole said a study of fossilized Galápagos corals offers “one more warning sign here of what we’re facing in a warmer world.” The research reconstructed a thousand-year ocean surface temperature record and found that the exceptional El Niño weather pattern has become stronger than at any point in that span.
“We’ve been seeing some very strong El Niño events in the late 20th and early 21st century, and what we didn’t know was how unusual those are,” Cole said. The team found that temperature variability since 1984 runs 36.5 percent higher than it did during 1000 to 1850 CE, and 16.2 percent higher than during 1851 to 1982.
Galápagos coral cores
Cole, an environmental scientist at the University of Michigan, led the work by analyzing fossilized Galápagos corals. The islands sit in the bullseye of the eastern Pacific ENSO pattern, and the corals grow one to two centimeters a year, which let the team sample coral cores millimeter by millimeter and pull more than a dozen measurements per year.
The researchers examined the strontium-to-calcium ratio and oxygen isotopes in coral skeletons because both track temperature. Living coral colonies cover recent decades and can be checked against instrument data, while dead coral heads can be dated using uranium-thorium methods to within a few years, even as far back as 500 years. Cole said, “We were also able to find corals that are dead and washed up on the beach.”
What the coral record showed
The team found 28 time-separated coral series from five islands covering scattered years back to around 1100 CE. Cole said, “The events don’t look anything like what we see in the pre-industrial era.” In the reconstructed record, events that once ran a degree or two above normal in the Galápagos now run three or four, and the corals also show a shift in skewness toward the positive direction.
Cole described that shift this way: “The skewness turned positive.”
ENSO, Peru, and Australia
El Niño and La Niña are the warm and cold swings of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the largest source of year-to-year climate variation on Earth. In practical terms, that means the pattern can shift rainfall across the tropics, dry out Australia, flood parts of Peru, and rearrange weather on most of the planet.
The study addresses a basic comparison with the past: whether the very strong El Niño events seen in recent decades are normal variation or something outside the preindustrial range. Cole said the coral record points toward the latter, but the reconstruction does not settle how much of the increase comes from natural variability versus warming.
For readers in places shaped by El Niño swings, the useful takeaway is not just that the modern pattern looks stronger. It is that the long coral record now gives climate scientists a benchmark that reaches far beyond the short instrument era, and that benchmark puts the last four decades in a different category from the centuries before them.

title: Nepal rescue hopes dim as death toll passes 1200
all_text:
Hopes of finding more survivors among thousands still missing in Nepal are fading, but authorities believe dozens of workers trapped in the tunnels of hydropower projects hit by the Himalayan catastrophe could still be alive.
It has been one week since the glacier collapse in the Himalayas unleashed flash floods that devastated the mountainous nation, killing at least 1204 people and leaving more than 4200 others missing - at least 38 of those Australians.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said his government was focusing on rehabilitation and rebuilding efforts while continuing to look for survivors among the thousands still missing.
The possibility of finding survivors was fading, authorities said, but there was no let up in rescue operations as teams scoured the mountainside along the border with China.
Major rescue operations were under way at tunnels at four hydropower projects and two of them with a total of nearly 100 people missing offered the strongest hopes of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside.
Authorities said powerhouses of hydroelectric plants have spaces and rooms for people to stay and rescuers are trying to reach them and look for survivors, with at least 639 people still missing, including those believed to be trapped in tunnels.
Specialised rescue teams from India, China and the United States were involved in the tunnel rescue attempts.
An army officer involved in the search-and-rescue operation, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the search would continue to look for survivors.
"All the tunnels are being searched with the assistance of experts from India, South Korea and China," he said.
"The search-and-rescue operation will continue as long as there is any hope of finding survivors. Even if there are no survivors, we will recover the dead bodies."
Progress has been hampered by persistent rain and challenging terrain, as crews have to work in a narrow mountain gorge, hemmed in between unstable cliffs and a fast-flowing river.
China will send more DNA identification experts and emergency supplies including Bailey bridges, mortuary refrigerators and communications equipment to Nepal to help with the rescue and relief efforts, the foreign ministry said.
Residents in Nepal's affected areas walked around the remains of what were once bustling villages and towns, trying to salvage whatever they could of their belongings.
Authorities in Nepal have been burying recovered bodies in temporary graves until they can be identified. They are preserving DNA samples, photographing distinguishing facial features and recording other identifying details to help match the remains with missing people and eventually return them to their families.
Children in Nuwakot and Rasuwa areas are increasingly showing signs of psychological distress after witnessing the fury of the flood last week, international charity Save the Children said in a statement.
Many minors told Save the Children that they are fearful and anxious after witnessing wide-ranging horrors including school buses full of friends washed away, their homes submerged and everything they hold dear carried away by the waters, the charity said.
Authorities in disaster-hit districts were working to restore regular routines as much as possible, with a special focus on getting children into makeshift schools.
At least 22,000 children urgently need safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene support, UNICEF said in a statement.
"Our priority is to restore normal life. We are considering if children can be taught in the holding centres till the time regular classes resume," said Phanindra Paudel, an official at Nepal's National Emergency Operation Centre.
with AP
Australian Associated Press

Hiteswar Saikia Foundation extends relief to flood-hit families in Nazira
NAZIRA, September 3, 2026 — The devastating July 19 flood caused by the Dikhow River inundated large parts of the Nazira Assembly constituency, severely affecting thousands of people and damaging homes and household belongings across several areas.
Among the worst-affected areas were Nepali Khuti, Kamalchapori, Tengahola, Santak, Shiloni Bihubar, Rajapul, Duwara Gaon, Khanikar Gaon, Ligiripukhuri, Ligiripukhuri Naga Gaon, Chumonibari, Hridayatpur and Hulangkatani in Bihubar.
Amid the post-flood hardship, the Hiteswar Saikia Foundation has come forward with relief assistance for affected and distressed families.
Former Nazira MLA and former Leader of the Opposition in the Assam Legislative Assembly, Debabrata Saikia, his wife Bandana Saikia, and Dr Hemaprabha Saikia, president of the Hiteswar Saikia Foundation, participated in the initiative to dispatch essential relief materials to flood-affected areas under Borbarua Panchayat.
As part of the humanitarian initiative, the foundation distributed folding beds, mattresses, pillows, bedsheets and essential cooking utensils to families whose household belongings were damaged or washed away in the flood.
According to the foundation, the relief effort is particularly aimed at supporting vulnerable sections of the affected population, including senior citizens, sick and ailing persons, and young children.
The initiative has provided much-needed assistance to families struggling to recover from the flood and rebuild their homes and livelihoods.

Inside the failed mission to eliminate FEMA
all_text:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency is no longer in the Trump administration's crosshairs, according to its former leader.
President Trump has made no secret of his disdain for the country's top disaster agency. In the first week of his second term, he attacked FEMA, saying, "I think, frankly, FEMA is not good," arguing that the agency should be eliminated. That rhetoric was echoed by top administration officials, including then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, who controlled the agency's budget.
Other federal agencies have since been stripped down or even eliminated, including the Department of Education, Voice of America and USAID.
But despite his own significant efforts to dismantle FEMA, the man who ran the agency at the time says FEMA isn't going anywhere.
"I think they're probably in a go-along-to-get-along kind of mode," says David Richardson, who led FEMA as acting administrator for much of 2025 and has since left the federal government. "I don't see there being a whole lot of change."
That shift is apparent inside the agency. In recent months, the fear of wholesale agency abolition or mass layoffs has dissipated among FEMA workers, according to multiple current FEMA employees who requested anonymity because they fear retaliation for speaking to a journalist. But the attempts to kill it have compounded some of FEMA's longstanding problems, like understaffing and delays in getting disaster recovery money to survivors.
"Looking back, I think what we saw was an ill-advised attempt to reduce the size of FEMA without fully understanding all the different functions that the agency has," says Andrew Rumbach, who studies disaster policy at the nonprofit Urban Institute.
A recent report from the Government Accountability Office raised concerns about whether the agency is adequately staffed. Parts of the agency that handle disaster recovery are still understaffed and struggling to get long-delayed money to disaster-stricken states, according to the FEMA employees who spoke to NPR.
It's only now that "serious reform efforts" are potentially on the horizon for the agency, Rumbach says, and those efforts no longer include eliminating it.
In response to questions from NPR about whether the agency's goals have changed since the president took office, a FEMA spokesperson wrote in an email, "FEMA remains fully operational and focused on its core mission of helping people before, during, and after disasters. As a matter of policy, we do not comment on accounts in forthcoming books, internal operational deliberations, or personnel matters." The White House declined to comment.
An inside account of the mission to eliminate FEMA
In one of his first interviews since leaving the agency late last year, Richardson sat down with NPR to talk about his time at FEMA and what he saw as his mission while he was there.
Richardson, who served as an artillery officer in the U.S. Marines for more than 20 years, arrived in FEMA's top job "reluctantly" and with no experience with disaster management. "FEMA's not my thing," he says.
Still, he says he was ready to take on the job because he had previously led efforts to cut the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction office within DHS.
"There was resentment towards FEMA. The president's intent was to shut it down or drastically reform it, and my predecessor wasn't moving fast enough in that direction," he says. "I went there for three things: to get FEMA through hurricane season, either shut it down or drastically reduce its size, and get it ready for rebranding."
Richardson says he arrived at FEMA in May 2025 with a plan to cut the number of employees at FEMA headquarters from about 6,000 to no more than 2,000 by November 2025.
"I always think that you can do more with less people, to a degree. At some point it's self-defeating. But it's definitely self-defeating to have too many people," says Richardson. "I'm a small-government person."
Deanne Criswell, who ran FEMA for four years under the Biden administration, says Richardson's description of FEMA as bloated and in need of drastic cuts suggests he does not understand the agency he briefly ran. She agrees that there are personnel changes that could make FEMA more efficient and effective, but "you can't just indiscriminately cut," she says. "It's only going to hurt the person who has the most need after a disaster."
The Trump administration's approach to cutting FEMA's spending and staffing has also struggled in the face of court challenges. An early attempt by the Trump administration to end a major grant program for disaster preparedness failed after a court challenge, and temporary workers who were terminated earlier this year are suing the agency. This summer, FEMA started rehiring many of those who were terminated.
"Dave, things have changed"
Within months of taking over the agency, Richardson realized that, as he puts it, "the focus was quickly shifting."
He says DHS leadership did not approve a plan he shared to downsize FEMA starting at the end of October 2025, one month before the end of the Atlantic hurricane season. Meanwhile, the president appointed a council of emergency experts to make recommendations about how to reform the agency, and Richardson says he started to wonder if the administration's goals had changed.
In July 2025, he says, he got his answer. As he recounts in a new book, Texas Flood: Power, Money, Politics, History, Bureaucracy and Tragedy, a DHS deputy chief of staff told him, "Dave, things have changed," before explaining that the president's council, not Richardson, would decide the future of FEMA.
Indeed, at public meetings of the council that summer, members discussed a variety of recommendations for whether and how to cut FEMA's workforce. At those meetings, emergency managers from powerful states led by Republican governors, including Texas and Florida, discussed the importance of reforming FEMA, but did not publicly advocate for eliminating it.
"I think that's where we started to see the rhetoric start to change about FEMA," says Criswell. "There are so many communities, and many Republican communities, that depend on the aid that you couldn't just get rid of it without having a negative impact."
The politics began to look more complicated, says Richardson. He writes that he supported the work of the council and continued to advocate for major cuts to FEMA, but "over the next few months, each time I received a call from DHS HQ complaining about the size of FEMA, I reminded them I could cut the size of the agency's HQ in half the next day; I only needed the green light."
Richardson says he never got the green light to make major cuts to FEMA staff.
New leadership and new reforms
Richardson resigned from FEMA in late 2025, and Noem was fired in March of this year.
Noem's replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, was previously a senator from Oklahoma and has extensive experience working with FEMA after major disasters in the state, Rumbach points out. Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to lead FEMA. Hamilton had previously served as the agency's acting administrator before Richardson took over, but Richardson felt he "wasn't moving fast enough."
In his introductory email to FEMA staff, obtained by NPR, Hamilton wrote that he looks forward to "strengthening the agency for the future."
Meanwhile, the president's FEMA Review Council submitted its recommendations earlier this year and called for states to take more responsibility for disasters. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Hamilton promised to come up with a plan to implement some of those recommendations. Just this week, the agency announced a pilot program with the state of Indiana aimed at getting disaster relief money to the state more quickly for flood repairs.
Rumbach says that approach is very different from Richardson's. "Those are the kind of improvements I'd hope to see in the coming years," he says. "Compared to some of the more dramatic and draconian cuts that were being recommended."
But many of the most sweeping FEMA reforms, such as making the agency report directly to the president and overhauling the system for getting money to individual disaster survivors, would require the White House and Congress to work together. That doesn't appear to be a priority for the administration today. A bipartisan FEMA reform bill is waiting in committee, and President Trump has rarely spoken about FEMA this summer, even after major disasters, including floods and catastrophic wildfires.

title: DVC starts issuing flood alerts for parts of Bengal after water release from two reservoirs
all_text:
The Damodar Valley Corporation has started issuing flood alerts for downstream areas in parts of West Bengal as it released a large volume of water from its Maithon and Panchet reservoirs, amid heavy rain, officials said on Thursday.
The combined water release by DVC on Wednesday evening was 1.2 lakh cusec from Panchet and Maithon dams.
The discharge of water was due to heavy rain in the catchment areas and increased inflow from Jharkhand's Tenughat dam, the officials said.
The flood alerts have been issued by DVC, an official said, adding that Purba Bardhaman, Paschim Bardhaman, Bankura, Hooghly and Howrah districts will be affected by the DVC water release.
The Damodar Valley Reservoir Regulation Committee (DVRRC) decided to release water from Maithon and Panchet reservoirs on Wednesday evening until further orders.
"The DVC has alerted the West Bengal government, district administrations and the additional district magistrate in Asansol, asking them to take precautionary measures in riverbank areas and remain prepared for possible flooding in the lower Damodar basin," an official said.
The decision to release water was taken to manage the rising pressure on the two reservoirs caused by heavy rainfall in their catchment areas and additional inflow from Tenughat dam, he said.
The quantum of discharge may be reviewed depending on changes in rainfall and inflow conditions, another official said.
The DVC has faced repeated criticism from the previous Mamata Banerjee government over flooding in the state's lower Damodar basin during periods of heavy rainfall and water release.
DVC officials, however, remain optimistic that the corporation will not be singled out during the current BJP regime, pointing out that water-release decisions are taken by the DVRRC, which also has representatives of the West Bengal government.
The committee regulates water release based on reservoir levels, inflows, rainfall forecasts and other technical considerations, officials said.
The DVC has maintained that controlled release of water is necessary for dam safety and to manage excess inflow into the reservoirs.
With substantial water being released from Maithon and Panchet, the authorities in downstream areas have been asked to closely monitor the river and vulnerable locations, the officials said.

title: Nepal rescue hopes dim as death toll passes 1200
all_text:
Hopes of finding more survivors among thousands still missing in Nepal are fading, but authorities believe dozens of workers trapped in the tunnels of hydropower projects hit by the Himalayan catastrophe could still be alive.
It has been one week since the glacier collapse in the Himalayas unleashed flash floods that devastated the mountainous nation, killing at least 1204 people and leaving more than 4200 others missing - at least 38 of those Australians.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said his government was focusing on rehabilitation and rebuilding efforts while continuing to look for survivors among the thousands still missing.
The possibility of finding survivors was fading, authorities said, but there was no let up in rescue operations as teams scoured the mountainside along the border with China.
Major rescue operations were under way at tunnels at four hydropower projects and two of them with a total of nearly 100 people missing offered the strongest hopes of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside.
Authorities said powerhouses of hydroelectric plants have spaces and rooms for people to stay and rescuers are trying to reach them and look for survivors, with at least 639 people still missing, including those believed to be trapped in tunnels.
Specialised rescue teams from India, China and the United States were involved in the tunnel rescue attempts.
An army officer involved in the search-and-rescue operation, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the search would continue to look for survivors.
"All the tunnels are being searched with the assistance of experts from India, South Korea and China," he said.
"The search-and-rescue operation will continue as long as there is any hope of finding survivors. Even if there are no survivors, we will recover the dead bodies."
Progress has been hampered by persistent rain and challenging terrain, as crews have to work in a narrow mountain gorge, hemmed in between unstable cliffs and a fast-flowing river.
China will send more DNA identification experts and emergency supplies including Bailey bridges, mortuary refrigerators and communications equipment to Nepal to help with the rescue and relief efforts, the foreign ministry said.
Residents in Nepal's affected areas walked around the remains of what were once bustling villages and towns, trying to salvage whatever they could of their belongings.
Authorities in Nepal have been burying recovered bodies in temporary graves until they can be identified. They are preserving DNA samples, photographing distinguishing facial features and recording other identifying details to help match the remains with missing people and eventually return them to their families.
Children in Nuwakot and Rasuwa areas are increasingly showing signs of psychological distress after witnessing the fury of the flood last week, international charity Save the Children said in a statement.
Many minors told Save the Children that they are fearful and anxious after witnessing wide-ranging horrors including school buses full of friends washed away, their homes submerged and everything they hold dear carried away by the waters, the charity said.
Authorities in disaster-hit districts were working to restore regular routines as much as possible, with a special focus on getting children into makeshift schools.
At least 22,000 children urgently need safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene support, UNICEF said in a statement.
"Our priority is to restore normal life. We are considering if children can be taught in the holding centres till the time regular classes resume," said Phanindra Paudel, an official at Nepal's National Emergency Operation Centre.
with AP

title: Floods hit a historic Grand Canyon lodge. It’s the second park landmark affected by a natural disaster in the past year - Local News 8
all_text:
By Chris Boyette, CNN
(CNN) — The Grand Canyon’s vast, mile-deep landscape may appear timeless, but two devastating disasters have recently struck the iconic natural wonder as the climate crisis intensifies extreme weather.
Muddy brown floodwaters roared through Phantom Ranch on August 29, swamping the 1920s lodge that has welcomed adventurers seeking a rare chance to spend the night at the bottom of the Grand Canyon and making it the park’s second historic structure impacted by a natural disaster in just over a year.
In July 2025, a destructive wildfire tore through dense pines on the canyon’s northern edge, destroying the historic Grand Canyon Lodge — the park’s only lodging there. The disastrous late-August flash flooding near Phantom Ranch struck below the burn scar left by that blaze, the National Weather Service said.
The climate crisis is making certain types of extreme weather events both more frequent and more severe. A warmer atmosphere can hold more water, which it wrings out in the form of more intense rainfall in some regions, potentially leading to devastating flooding. It’s also loading the dice in favor of wildfires that burn longer and hotter. In turn, landscapes marred by fire are more susceptible to flash flooding, due to sparse vegetation and changes in the soil.
Ahead of the normally busy Labor Day weekend at the park, the scars of these natural disasters and subsequent closures of lodging and hiking trails will likely impact how visitors enjoy one of America’s most iconic landscapes during the holiday and for years to come.
Floodwaters swamp a remote refuge at the bottom of the Grand Canyon
Tucked beside the Bright Angel Creek, nearly a mile below the canyon rim, Phantom Ranch was built in 1922. Construction was carried out mostly by foot and mules, as documented by historical photographs from the National Park Service.
To this day, there are no roads leading to the ranch. Guests arrive only by a 7.5-to-10-mile hike, mule ride or rafting down the Colorado River, making it one of the most remote and sought-after reservations in the National Park system, with reservations available via an online lottery 15 months in advance.
The stone cabins and canteen made of rounded river rocks showcase the rustic, homey appeal of the campground, whose outward appearance had changed little since 1922, according to the NPS.
The remote ranch’s hallmark isolation is now complicating recovery efforts.
As the murky waters of Bright Angel Creek began to retreat after the floods, witnesses described debris-filled water carrying mud, rocks and fallen trees through the canyon, transforming the area surrounding the ranch.
Floods destroyed the footbridges, leaving remnants of stone pylons littering the creek, NPS said, and hiking trails, utilities and other infrastructure suffered significant damage.
The ranch, the nearby Bright Angel Campground and large sections of the inner canyon trail network remain closed indefinitely.
The NPS is cleaning up the campground and assessing damage to facilities and infrastructure across the area, but it is too soon to determine the extent of the damage at Phantom Ranch, the Interior Department said in a statement to CNN.
Two people were killed in the flooding, and another hiker remains missing.
After the flood, 62 people were evacuated from the campground and the lower North Kaibab Trail, according to the NPS.
One factor that may have limited the disaster’s toll was the closure of the ranch’s hiker dormitories. The bunkhouses had been closed since early 2020 because of the Covid-19 pandemic and subsequent infrastructure projects, with one men’s dorm and one women’s dorm scheduled to reopen September 1. Had they been full, more hikers could have been caught in the rising waters.
A wildfire destroyed the park’s sole North Rim lodging
A lightning strike on July 4, 2025, sparked a blaze fueled by hot temperatures, low humidity and strong winds that raced across the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park. Within days, it had destroyed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge.
Park officials initially expressed little concern about the fire at the less-visited North Rim, which draws only about a tenth of the Grand Canyon’s millions of annual visitors. But by July 13, the Dragon Bravo Fire had grown out of control, destroying 85% of the lodge and its outbuildings, according to the NPS.
When the lodge burned down in 2025, it wasn’t the first time. First built in 1928, the lodge burned down in a kitchen fire in 1932 and was rebuilt in 1937, according to the Grand Canyon Historical Society. The new building used much of the original lodge’s native Kaibab Limestone, according to the NPS.
Located at the end of Arizona’s Highway 67, the Grand Canyon Lodge welcomed travelers and was often their first sight in the park — even before the canyon itself, the NPS said.
Its sloped roof and large ponderosa beams made it a landmark on the North Rim.
The NPS said long-term recovery planning is underway, but no reopening date has been announced for the historic lodge.
One famous resident of the lodge survived the flames. Brighty the Burro, a 600-pound bronze statue that greeted visitors in the Grand Canyon Lodge, was found damaged by the fire, but park officials chose to save the cherished mascot.
The statue was modeled after a real burro that lived in the canyon in the early 20th century. According to the Grand Canyon Historical Society, the animal gave children rides and hauled water to a North Ridge summer camp in exchange for pancakes.
Brighty is being kept safe at the Grand Canyon Museum Collection facility, the NPS said, with no timeline yet for his restoration or return to the North Rim.

title: Fundraiser set up for downtown business impacted by water main break
all_text:
SPRINGFIELD, IL – After months of preparation and a soft opening one day before disaster, The Bus Stop on Monroe Street is taking a detour down to Fifth Street to help fundraise to stay opening following a water main break last month.
A 24-inch cast iron transmission water pipe burst in downtown Springfield on Aug. 27 causing severe flood damage to several adjacent businesses on Monroe Street heading toward the Post Office to the city municipal building.
One of the businesses worst the hit, The Bus Stop, was about to be a new bar and nightlife entertainment spot serving cocktail drinks with an open mic to bring "live music back downtown."
The water main break caused the basement at the business to flood over five feet in two hours as transmission water rushed inwards through the foundation, causing severe damage to both the business and building.
A fundraiser to help fund the business to get back on route will be held Sept. 4 at Fifth Street GEM at 221 S. Fifth St. from 5 to 10 p.m.
Entry is a $5 donation with a 50/50 raffle, merch table and donations available via CashApp to '$thebusstop217'. Ward 5 Ald. Lakeisha Purchase, who represents most of downtown constituents, owns Fifth Street GEM, which also flooded the night of the water main burst.
Shirts can be purchased for $25 to support the Bus Stop on the companies Facebook page.
Zac Lowman, one of the four owners of The Bus Stop, told The State Journal-Register on Aug. 31 their insurance company, Society Insurance, would not cover the damage to the water from an outside source of the building and it is considered an exclusion.
For Lowman, who spoke to The SJ-R back in June, the bar was a dream his mother had he wanted to accomplish. All the men tied to the bar Michael Howard, Trevor Minton and Aaron Phillips had a dream tied to the business.
"We have no power. It's just a freak thing so I've had to process what are the odds of this happening," Lowman said. "We had a pretty good momentum for the grand opening."
Lowman estimates under the LLC the group of owners have invested close to over $30,000 into the business.
Insurance coverage on the building itself is still being determined by adjusters, Lowman said. He also said that the broker from Diamond Bros. Insurance who is working on the insurance claim for the building and business separately told him on Sept. 1 both insurance companies are going to deny the claims for the building suffering up to six figures in damage.
If the building is deemed uninsurable, funds from the fundraiser will go toward reopening in a new building, hopefully somewhere downtown, Lowman said.
Lowman said the city provided the business forms to start an insurance claim to see what they can do, but could not share more information at time of publication.
Next door neighbors reopened
Businesses next door to The Bus Stop, Gallina's Pizza and Dumb Records reopened the Aug. 28, with an employee from Gallina's saying there was not significant damage.
Brian Galecki, who co-owns Dumb Records with Jeff Black, told The State Journal-Register their business has yet to file an insurance claim for their business and for the time being have closed down part of their store to allow cleanup of the basement.
More: Water main break floods downtown Springfield streets
The green "BRAT" elephant has taken a vacation out of the private eye while work is done on the street.
Galecki said they are not sure if they plan on filing an insurance claim once they drag all the inventory out to the dumpster they've rented, but said the big loss so far has been in foot traffic with the road closed.
The second store, Dumber Records inside the White Oaks Mall, is still open and carrying inventory.

title: Daily weather tracker: Heavy rain threatens Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal; flood risk rises
all_text:
Summary
Madhya Pradesh faces extremely heavy rainfall, with red alerts issued as flooding, waterlogging and rising river levels threaten several districts.
Eastern Uttar Pradesh remains under orange alert, with intense rainfall potentially triggering flash floods across several districts during the next 24 hours.
West Bengal and Sikkim may receive very heavy rainfall, raising concerns over flooding, landslides and disruptions in mountainous and riverine areas.
Delhi, Haryana, Punjab, Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh could witness heavy showers, while landslides and traffic disruptions remain possible in hilly regions.
Thunderstorms, lightning and strong winds are expected across several states, prompting authorities and residents to remain cautious during severe weather conditions.
Several parts of central, northern and eastern India are bracing for intense rainfall as multiple weather systems remain active across the region. According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD) bulletin issued on September 3, a low-pressure area over northeast Madhya Pradesh and adjoining regions continues to influence weather conditions, bringing widespread rain, thunderstorms and the possibility of extremely heavy downpours.
The weather system is expected to move west-northwestwards during the next 24 hours. Its movement could intensify rainfall over southern Uttar Pradesh and northern Madhya Pradesh, with several areas likely to experience thunderstorms and spells of intense rain.
The monsoon trough is also active, extending across several parts of the country and passing through the centre of the low-pressure area before reaching Jharkhand and the coastal region near Digha. An active western disturbance is adding to the complex weather pattern, increasing the likelihood of unsettled conditions across northern and central India.
Eastern Madhya Pradesh remains the area of greatest concern. The IMD has warned of heavy to very heavy rainfall, with isolated locations potentially receiving more than 204.5 mm of rain. Red and orange alerts have been issued for different areas as the possibility of severe waterlogging and flooding increases.
Several locations have already recorded substantial rainfall. Satna received 90 mm, Jabalpur 70 mm and Sagar 60 mm during the preceding 24-hour period. Continued rainfall could push water levels higher in small rivers, streams and drains, particularly in low-lying areas.
Authorities and residents have been advised to closely monitor local weather conditions and move to safer locations if flooding begins.
Eastern Uttar Pradesh is also facing a significant weather threat. Districts including Prayagraj, Varanasi, Mirzapur, Sonbhadra, Jaunpur, Fatehpur, Kaushambi, Banda and Chitrakoot could receive between 115.6 mm to 204.4 mm of rainfall.
The IMD has issued orange alerts for several areas and warned of flash-flood conditions during the next 24 hours. Persistent heavy rain could cause extensive waterlogging in fields, roads and residential areas. Mahoba, Jhansi and Lalitpur in western Uttar Pradesh are also being watched for the possibility of sudden flooding.
Residents living near rivers, streams and vulnerable low-lying areas have been urged to exercise extreme caution.
Heavy to very heavy rainfall is expected across parts of Sikkim and sub-Himalayan West Bengal. Rainfall of 115.6 mm to 204.4 mm is possible in some locations, raising concerns in mountainous and river-adjacent areas.
The risk is particularly serious in hilly terrain, where intense rain can trigger landslides, disrupt roads and affect local transport. Kolkata's Alipore recorded 80 mm of rain during the past 24 hours, underlining the strength of the ongoing weather activity.
Rainfall is also expected over Delhi, Haryana, Chandigarh, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and parts of western Uttar Pradesh. Yellow alerts have been issued for several areas, where 64.5 mm to 115.5 mm of rain could occur.
In Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, heavy showers may lead to landslides, road disruptions and localized flooding. Commuters and travellers in vulnerable mountainous areas are advised to remain alert and avoid unnecessary journeys during periods of intense rainfall.
The unsettled weather is accompanied by a risk of lightning across Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Uttarakhand, West Bengal and western Uttar Pradesh. Andhra Pradesh may experience thunderstorms accompanied by winds reaching 40–50 kmph, while Telangana, interior Karnataka, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh could see winds of 30–40 kmph.
Bihar and several northeastern states, including Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura, are also expected to receive heavy rain in isolated areas.
With more rain expected, farmers have been advised to ensure proper drainage in fields and remove excess water from low-lying agricultural land. Irrigation should be suspended until conditions improve, while harvested crops and agricultural produce should be moved to safe, dry locations.
The coming 24 hours are likely to be crucial for parts of Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. Residents are advised to remain weather-aware, avoid flooded roads and waterways, and stay indoors or in safe shelters during thunderstorms and lightning.

title: Nepalis pin hopes on 'wall of the missing' in hunt for relatives after deadly flood | The Express Tribune
all_text:
Nepalis pin hopes on 'wall of the missing' in hunt for relatives after deadly flood
Some pictures are embedded in posters meticulously filled in with details of missing persons, contact numbers
Sati Sigdel makes daily visits to a hospital wall in Kathmandu blanketed in hundreds of photographs, some of missing relatives, others of retrieved bodies yet to be identified, in desperate hopes of finding news of her cousin.
"We put up her photo three days ago, but we still haven't heard anything," Sigdel said of her cousin, Sweety Paithan, one of more than 4,200 missing after a catastrophic flood triggered by a glacier collapse killed more than 1,200 people.
Hopes for survivors are dimming steadily more than a week after the disaster, although Nepali authorities are keeping up relentless search efforts, with some 900 feared trapped in hydroelectric power plants.
Late on Wednesday, a handful of people from across mountainous Nepal were carefully scanning the pictures on the wall at the capital's Tribhuvan University teaching hospital, and asking nearby guards if they had heard their names.
"We're hoping for a miracle," said Sapna Neupane, who was hoping to make contact with her maternal uncle's family of four, all missing. "It's hard just to stand in front of this wall, looking at thousands of pictures."
Some pictures are embedded in posters meticulously filled in with details of the missing and contact numbers, while others are handwritten scribbles under photographs.
In one, the word "Missing" is emblazoned above the heads of a couple standing beside each other. Another depicts a muscular young man, with a close-up of a left-arm tattoo, probably to help identify him.
At the nearby Pashupatinath Temple on the banks of the Bagmati River, some families were cremating straw effigies, having given up hope after unsuccessful searches for their relatives.
"It weighs heavily on my heart," said Tapindra Prasad Timalsina, as a Hindu priest chanted prayers while others poured water on an effigy of his relative, 21-year-old Sabin, before lighting the pyre, in a rite typically reserved for the dead.
Back at the wall, hope was undimmed for Sigdel, however, in her vigil maintained since Monday.
"I come here every day with my relatives and friends, hoping for news," she said.

title: North Odisha flood situation grim; 373 villages inundated
all_text:
North Odisha flood situation grim; 373 villages inundated
 Prefer HTon Google
Bhubaneswar, Sept 3 The flood situation in north Odisha remained grim on Thursday, even as water levels in major rivers showed a receding trend after inundating parts of Balasore, Jajpur and Mayurbhanj districts, officials said.
The Subarnarekha, which inundated 214 villages across five blocks of Balasore district Bhograi, Baliapal, Basta, Remuna and Jaleshwar was flowing above the danger mark but showed a falling trend, they said.
"As of noon, the water level of Subarnarekha at Rajghat stood at 10.84 metres against the danger level of 10.36 metres and is currently showing a falling trend, indicating gradual improvement in the river situation," Water Resources Department's engineer-in-chief Dilip Kumar Rout said.
Around 35,740 people from affected villages in Balasore district have been evacuated and housed in 72 relief shelters, the official said.
The situation in Jajpur and Mayurbhanj districts also remained grim due to flooding in the Baitarani and its tributaries, including the Salandi and Budhabalanga rivers.
"In Jajpur, 62 villages remained inundated in Dasarathpur block. A total of 22 relief camps are operational, covering 7,745 beneficiaries," the official said.
In Mayurbhanj, people in 97 villages and two wards of Baripada Municipality have been affected. A total of 29 relief camps are operational, providing shelter to 10,501 beneficiaries.
As many as 104 houses have been reported damaged, and nine polythene rolls have been distributed in the district, officials said.
According to an official statement, water levels in several other rivers, including the Mahanadi at Naraj, Ib at Sundargarh, Brahmani at Panposh, Baitarani at Anandpur and Akhuapada, Budhabalanga at NH-5, Vansadhara at Gunupur and Jalaka at Mathani, were also showing a falling trend on Thursday morning.
Authorities at the Hirakud reservoir are discharging excess water into the Mahanadi through four sluice gates. The water level in the reservoir stood at 627.29 feet against the full reservoir level of 630 feet.
In view of the flood situation, the administration has deployed 47 rescue teams, comprising 21 Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force teams, four National Disaster Response Force teams and 22 Fire and Emergency Services teams.
Jajpur has three ODRAF teams deployed, while Mayurbhanj has six ODRAF and 13 Fire and Emergency Services teams. In Balasore, which is among the worst-affected districts, 12 ODRAF, four NDRF and nine Fire and Emergency Services teams have been deployed for rescue and response operations.
Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department , in its latest bulletin, said a well-marked low-pressure area over northeast Madhya Pradesh and adjoining areas was likely to move west-northwestwards across south Uttar Pradesh and adjoining north Madhya Pradesh during the next 24 hours.
The IMD forecast thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and winds of 30-40 kmph at one or two places in Balasore, Bhadrak, Jajpur, Kendrapara, Jagatsinghpur, Cuttack, Keonjhar and Mayurbhanj districts.
The state government has asked district administrations to remain alert to the possibility of localised flooding, waterlogging in low-lying areas, closure of underpasses and damage to roads and vulnerable structures.
Authorities have also been directed to remain vigilant about possible damage to horticulture and standing crops due to heavy rainfall or flooding. Relief and support measures will continue in affected areas until normalcy is restored.
The State Emergency Operation Centre under the Office of the Special Relief Commissioner is monitoring the situation round the clock in coordination with all District Emergency Operation Centres .
"The improving river situation and reduced rainfall activity are encouraging signs," Special Relief Commissioner Rajesh P Patil said.
He, however, said the state government continued to maintain a high level of preparedness, with round-the-clock monitoring, coordinated field response and necessary relief and restoration measures being undertaken to ensure that support reaches affected communities without delay.
This article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.

title: Australian drones, telco data sent to help Nepal search
all_text:
Telecommunication data is being provided to Nepali authorities to help narrow down the last known locations of Australians missing after catastrophic floods, as specialised drones from NSW are deployed to the disaster zone.
Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong said concerns deepened every day for the 38 missing Australians, as the death toll surpasses 1200.
Rescue teams from the Nepali army were expected to conduct searches on foot with helicopter and drone support in locations where many Australians were believed to have been staying, Senator Wong said.
The dozens of Australians are among 4200 people missing after a glacier collapse near Nepal's border with China triggered devastating floods across towns and valleys.
"I can indicate that after our inquiries that Nepali authorities have advised us that searches are being conducted in the locations identified by Australia, including (The Kailash Hotel) and the Royal Himalaya Hotel amongst others," Senator Wong told reporters on Thursday.
A team of six drone operators and four incident management specialists from Fire and Rescue NSW will be sent to the Nepal flood zone with personnel from the Queensland Fire Department as part of additional on-the-ground support announced by the government on Thursday.
The 15-person Australian Disaster Assistance Response Team will use advanced drone technology for real-time imagery and geospatial information and mapping of affected regions, where transport routes and critical infrastructure remain severely damaged.
"They will play an important role, flying drones through areas deemed too dangerous for ground teams to search and providing critical information to guide search and rescue operations," Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell said.
The technology has AI capabilities that can help find victims, along with thermal imaging to identify trapped victims through heat sources.
Built-in speakers and spotlights will give emergency crews the opportunity to communicate with potentially trapped victims in the rugged and highly mountainous region.
DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and to contact next of kin where appropriate.
Nepali authorities will also be given telecommunication data to help narrow the last known location of missing Australians.
"We continue to work around the clock to ascertain as much information as we can and provide it to the families of missing Australians," Senator Wong said.
"We all hold on to hope, and we've got to hold on to hope."
There was no change in the number of missing Australians, after five citizens were confirmed safe on Wednesday.
Dedicated case officers are being assigned to next of kin, with disaster victim identification specialists ready to be deployed if needed.
Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.
More than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items.
Australians have donated more than $4 million to the Emergency Action Alliance to support recovery efforts.
The federal government will provide a further $3 million to match public donations, bringing the ongoing humanitarian support package to a total of $11 million.
Grieving community members in Australia continue to cling to hope their loved ones are safe.
"Lots of people are stuck in the tunnels over there as well, and most don't have any contact ... we are still hopeful that maybe we can get good news," Non-Resident Nepali Association Victorian co-ordinator Mahadev Dhanuk told AAP.
"Many are not personally affected, but culturally we feel like one family. That's why everyone is devastated," Mr Dhanuk said.
"All of the community is trying to overcome their own plight and trying to help and think how can we stand with Nepal?"
Australian Associated Press

title: 115k DTE customers without power as more severe weather moves through region
all_text:
Tens of thousands of homes and businesses in southeast Michigan were left without electricity after a series of late-night thunderstorms thundered through the region late Wednesday, Sept. 2.
Repairs have been slowed and additional outages are occurring as additional rounds of thunderstorms have moved through Oakland County late Thursday morning.
After another storm moved through Oakland County, the number of customers without power had grown to 115,650 by early afternoon Thursday. With wind gusts hitting 70 mph, sirens sounded in some communities, including Troy. In Oakland Township and Rochester Hills, branches were knocked down and water covered some roadways, including parts of Adams Road. The township warned that motorists should turn around and attempt to drive over water-covered roads.
The Orion Township Professional Firefighters Local reported at about noon on Facebook they had been “inundated with calls following the storm. Multiple power lines down, multiple trees down, and possible structure fires. Every station is committed on emergencies at the moment. Remember, if you see a line down, do not approach it and call 9-1-1. Please be vigilant of tree limbs and the potential for falling branches.”
In Rochester, the city’s police department reported at 1 p.m. Thursday, via Facebook, “Emergency operations are in place and we have crews from police, fire, and public works working diligently to get branches clear, downed wires safe, and return Rochester to normal travel.”
In Rochester Hills, power poles along Tienken Road in front of Adams High School were tilting over, leading to the road being closed, according to images shared on the Oakland County Scanner Facebook group.
The storms late Wednesday carried flooding downpours, 2-inch hail, and spectacular lightning followed by house-shaking thunder.
Metro Detroit was hardest hit area in regards to power outages.
Shortly after 9 a.m. Thursday, the number of DTE Energy customers in the dark numbered 99,020. Additionally, Consumers Energy reported 2,825 customers without power, including about 500 south of Midland and the rest southwest of Lansing.
DTE Energy officials said late in the morning that more than 2,600 storm response team members were working already to repair damage and restore electricity with another 80 en route from outside of the state to assist in restoration efforts.
“We estimate that 80 percent of impacted customers will be restored by the end of the day,” DTE said. “We know how challenging it is to be without power.”
The utility emphasized that workers are acting quickly but also will work as safely as possible. One issue to contend with is the potential for more severe weather on Thursday. At 10:50 a.m., the National Weather Service issued a severe thunderstorm warning with a storm system moving eastward through central Oakland County with wind gusts of 70 mph expected. The warning will last until 11:45 a.m.
“Expect considerable tree damage. Damage is likely to mobile homes, roofs, and outbuildings,” the NWS said. “People attending Michigan State Fair should seek safe shelter immediately!”
By 10 a.m., the number of outages for DTE Energy topped 101,800 customers before being reduced slightly to just over 99,000 an hour later.
Center Line Public Schools and Howell Public Schools had to cancel classes Thursday as did Brother Rice and Marian high schools due to power outages. According to wxyz.com, a large tree was toppled, crashing into a home. Also, WWJ-950 reported on a massive tree having been knocked onto a home in Warren.
There were no immediate reports of significant storm damage in Macomb or Oakland counties on Wednesday night, but that could change by Thursday morning in the light of day, according to the National Weather Service.
“The characteristics of this storm produced severe damaging winds produced as it moved through Livingston and Oakland counties and to the east through Macomb County,” said Alex Manion, a meteorologist with the weather service.
“We had reports of 67 mile an hour winds near the Livingston County airport and one of our employees lives in Livingston and he estimated wind gusts to be around 70 mph at the very least.”
In Macomb County, winds were between 45 and 60 mph during the storms, Manion said.
According to DTE’s outage map, more than 56,000 utility customers were without electricity early Thursday. The map showed pockets of Macomb County neighborhoods had no power.
As of 6 a.m. Thursday, DTE showed 81,500 customers without power with the highest concentrations between M-59 and I-96.
The county was under a severe thunderstorm warning late Wednesday. A flood warning was in effect until 5:30 a.m. Thursday for southwestern Macomb and southern Oakland counties as 2 inches of rain was expected.
Meteorologists said the region had a marginal risk of showers and strong thunderstorms for Thursday and Friday before the area dries out for a nice Labor Day weekend as the humid and hot conditions end. Highs between Saturday and Monday should be about 80 degrees.
DTE urged people to remember to stay at least 25 feet away from any downed power lines or anything in contact with them.

title: The Himalayas are the most densely dammed region in the world. Is their ‘green’ energy worth it?
all_text:
People work during a search and rescue operation near the Hydropower Project sites, following deadly flash floods and mudslides that hit parts of Nepal, in this handout provided by the Nepal army. (Reuters/Yonhap)
          Following catastrophic flooding and landslides in Nepal, experts say the destruction may have been exacerbated by the concentration of hydropower development in the Himalayas, including Korea South-East Power’s Upper Trishuli-1 project, which was heavily damaged in the flooding. That necessitates a careful examination of the potential issues that can arise at the junction of the intensifying climate crisis and the proliferation of hydropower plants seeking to harness the region’s abundant water resources.
More than 1,100 hydropower projects are being planned, built or operated across the “Asian Water Tower,” the source of water for 11 major rivers originating in the Hindu Kush Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau.
Nepal is particularly focused on hydropower development. It currently generates 3,167 megawatts of electricity at 166 plants, with plans to eventually generate 10,265 megawatts at 538 plants.
But amid recurring disasters such as earthquakes, floods and landslides due to glacier loss, concerns are mounting that dense clusters of small hydropower plants could increase landslide risks, degrade the catchment area and reduce water availability.
The International Finance Corporation (IFC), a World Bank affiliate that led private investment in Upper Trishuli-1, published an assessment back in 2020 about the cumulative impact on the Trishuli River Basin not of individual power plants, but of hydropower development as a whole.
The report warned that under a business-as-usual approach, the river basin’s “ecological integrity is predicted to decline to seriously/critically modified due to the combined impact of hydropower projects and resource extraction.”
Critics say, however, that appropriate measures were never taken.
Ideal conditions for high-altitude hydropower
The floods and landslides that struck the Himalayas on the Nepal-China border on Aug. 26 have killed more than 1,000 people to date and underscored numerous problems that had long been overlooked.
One of those issues is the high concentration of hydropower plants in the region.
Given how numerous such facilities are, hydropower damage is almost always mentioned after the floods and landslides that commonly occur in the Himalayas during the monsoon season, running from June to September.
Considering that the two basic requirements for hydropower generation are an abundant water supply and substantial differences in elevation, the jagged, ice-capped Himalayas are considered an ideal environment.
The problem is that there are now too many hydropower development projects.
The collapse of glacier ice and rock in Chamoli District in northern India’s Uttarakhand in 2021 triggered floods and landslides, severely damaging four hydropower plants, including one on the Rishiganga River.
A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) in the northeastern Indian state of Sikkim in October 2023 claimed more than 170 lives and completely destroyed the 1,200-megawatt Teesta-III hydropower plant, the largest in the region.
A magnitude 7.8 earthquake in Nepal’s Gorkha District in 2015 had a death toll of about 9,000 and knocked out 30% of the country’s hydropower generation.
The Hindu Kush Himalaya, the Tibetan Plateau and surrounding areas form the headwaters of 11 major rivers. The region provides water resources to as many as 3 billion people and supports global biodiversity, earning the moniker of the “Asian Water Tower.”
Analysts say that more than 1,100 hydropower plants have been planned or are being built or operated in the Asian Water Tower since 2000.
Although many of these plants are part of large-scale projects in China and India, countries such as Nepal and Bhutan have also invested in hydropower as a vehicle for national development or a source of export revenue.
“Economic viability, along with water volume and hydrostatic head, is an essential prerequisite for hydropower development,” said Hwang Seok-hwan, the head of the department of hydro science and engineering research at the Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology.
“That’s why mountainous countries facing resource scarcity in other areas have built large numbers of small hydropower plants in confined areas.”
Notably, Nepal has built numerous small hydropower plants (Upper Trishuli-1 being one of them) that divert part of a river’s flow through tunnels to exploit a difference in elevation.
But even minor projects can cause major problems when crammed into a small space.
“A small project by itself is unlikely to have a significant impact on the surrounding environment. But when multiple projects are concentrated in one area, they can collectively push the environment past a critical threshold,” Hwang said.
Yadu Pokhrel, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Michigan State University, wrote in a recent paper analyzing the threats facing the Asian Water Tower that “dense networks of small and diversion-type hydropower projects can cumulatively dewater or inundate river reaches, fragment habitats, alter flow regimes, and affect conservation lands.”
An aerial photo shows the washed-away Pasang Lhamu Highway along the side of the Trishuli River in Nepal on Aug. 31, 2026, following disastrous flooding there. (AP/Yonhap)
          An inflection point for hydropower concentration?
The IFC, the World Bank affiliate that led international financing for Upper Trishuli-1, published an impact assessment of hydropower development in the Trishuli River Basin in 2020. The report sought to assess the cumulative effects across the basin of multiple hydropower projects being developed and operated simultaneously.
“There are six operational hydropower projects along the Trishuli River and its major tributaries that total 81 megawatts (MW). In addition, seven hydropower projects (total of 286 MW) are under construction and at least 23 hydropower projects are in the planning stage,” the report said.
The report identified “aquatic habitat fragmentation, degradation of the catchment area, reduced water availability, and an increased risk of landslides” as major cumulative effects of hydropower development. It also warned that under a “business as usual” approach, “ecological integrity is predicted to decline to seriously/critically modified due to the combined impact of hydropower projects and resource extraction.”
More specifically, the report said that the upper basin, where hydropower projects are more economically viable, was likely to face particularly severe effects because multiple projects were being pursued both on the main river and in other areas.
Yet there is little sign that any measures were taken to address these risks during the actual development process.
The India-based nonprofit South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People criticized the IFC for its investment, saying it “had the opportunity and space to address cumulative disasters, GLOFs, transboundary impacts, compound disasters, [and the] growing footprint of a changing climate. It did nothing.”
“Funding was sought and provided in the garb of 'Climate and Disaster Resilience,’” the network said, yet still it made no effort to build an early warning system or other measures.
An analysis of the 2021 Chamoli disaster published by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, an intergovernmental body for the Himalaya region, said that the increasing intensity of disasters in mountain areas due to climate change has raised the question: “Is hydropower a boon or a bane?”
While hydropower is often touted as a form of “green” energy and a solution to the climate crisis, its development can have significant environmental impacts, including changes to river flows and water quality, while climate change is also increasing the risks posed by flow variability, extreme weather events and GLOFs.
“Infrastructure investments [. . .] [require] integrated governance approaches that recognize water, energy, and climate as fundamentally interconnected systems,” writes Pokhrel. “Securing the future of the [Asian Water Tower] will require reimagining infrastructure development — not just a rapid expansion to meet growing demands — under a shared vision of transboundary cooperation and system-level resilience.”
By Choi Won-hyung, staff reporter

title: Australian drones, telco data sent to help Nepal search
all_text:
Telecommunication data is being provided to Nepali authorities to help narrow down the last known locations of Australians missing after catastrophic floods, as specialised drones from NSW are deployed to the disaster zone.
Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong said concerns deepened every day for the 38 missing Australians, as the death toll surpasses 1200.
Rescue teams from the Nepali army were expected to conduct searches on foot with helicopter and drone support in locations where many Australians were believed to have been staying, Senator Wong said.
The dozens of Australians are among 4200 people missing after a glacier collapse near Nepal's border with China triggered devastating floods across towns and valleys.
"I can indicate that after our inquiries that Nepali authorities have advised us that searches are being conducted in the locations identified by Australia, including (The Kailash Hotel) and the Royal Himalaya Hotel amongst others," Senator Wong told reporters on Thursday.
A team of six drone operators and four incident management specialists from Fire and Rescue NSW will be sent to the Nepal flood zone with personnel from the Queensland Fire Department as part of additional on-the-ground support announced by the government on Thursday.
The 15-person Australian Disaster Assistance Response Team will use advanced drone technology for real-time imagery and geospatial information and mapping of affected regions, where transport routes and critical infrastructure remain severely damaged.
"They will play an important role, flying drones through areas deemed too dangerous for ground teams to search and providing critical information to guide search and rescue operations," Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell said.
The technology has AI capabilities that can help find victims, along with thermal imaging to identify trapped victims through heat sources.
Built-in speakers and spotlights will give emergency crews the opportunity to communicate with potentially trapped victims in the rugged and highly mountainous region.
DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and to contact next of kin where appropriate.
Nepali authorities will also be given telecommunication data to help narrow the last known location of missing Australians.
"We continue to work around the clock to ascertain as much information as we can and provide it to the families of missing Australians," Senator Wong said.
"We all hold on to hope, and we've got to hold on to hope."
There was no change in the number of missing Australians, after five citizens were confirmed safe on Wednesday.
Dedicated case officers are being assigned to next of kin, with disaster victim identification specialists ready to be deployed if needed.
Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.
More than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items.
Australians have donated more than $4 million to the Emergency Action Alliance to support recovery efforts.
The federal government will provide a further $3 million to match public donations, bringing the ongoing humanitarian support package to a total of $11 million.
Grieving community members in Australia continue to cling to hope their loved ones are safe.
"Lots of people are stuck in the tunnels over there as well, and most don't have any contact ... we are still hopeful that maybe we can get good news," Non-Resident Nepali Association Victorian co-ordinator Mahadev Dhanuk told AAP.
"Many are not personally affected, but culturally we feel like one family. That's why everyone is devastated," Mr Dhanuk said.
"All of the community is trying to overcome their own plight and trying to help and think how can we stand with Nepal?"
